homer_simpson.name: Homer Simpson
homer_simpson.desc:
The father of the Simpson family and safety inspector at Sector 7-G of the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant, a job for which he is conspicuously unqualified. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

In the earliest shorts and first season Homer is a gruff, exasperated father in the mould of a conventional sitcom dad; across the following seasons the writing shifted him towards the impulsive, appetite-driven figure that dominates the show, and the series increasingly built its plots around him rather than around Bart.

His annoyed grunt, written in scripts as an instruction rather than a word, became the catchphrase d'oh.

marge_simpson.name: Marge Simpson
marge_simpson.desc:
Homer's wife and the moral centre of the household, recognisable by her towering blue hair. Voiced by Julie Kavner, whose distinctive rasp the writers built the character's delivery around.

Marge is written as the family's stabilising force, forgiving Homer repeatedly while pursuing her own frustrated ambitions in episodes that hand her a career, an artistic streak or a political cause. Born Marge Bouvier, she met Homer in high school detention.

bart_simpson.name: Bart Simpson
bart_simpson.desc:
The ten-year-old eldest Simpson child, a self-styled underachiever whose pranks, prank calls to Moe's Tavern and chalkboard punishments defined the show's first years. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

By Matt Groening's account the name is an anagram of brat. Bart was the show's breakout figure in 1990, driving a merchandising boom around catchphrases such as eat my shorts and don't have a cow, man, before the series gradually redistributed its focus towards Homer.

lisa_simpson.name: Lisa Simpson
lisa_simpson.desc:
The eight-year-old middle child, a gifted student and baritone saxophone player who functions as the family's conscience and its intellectual outsider. Voiced by Yeardley Smith.

Lisa carries much of the show's earnest material: her isolation at school, her friendship with jazz musician Bleeding Gums Murphy, and the episodes in which she adopts convictions the series then kept. She became a vegetarian in 1995 and a Buddhist in 2001, and both changes were treated as permanent rather than reset at the end of the episode.

maggie_simpson.name: Maggie Simpson
maggie_simpson.desc:
The infant Simpson, almost always silent and never without her pacifier. Her rare spoken words are treated as events, notably in Lisa's First Word, where her first word is voiced by Elizabeth Taylor.

Maggie carries two of the show's best-known plot turns: she is revealed as the shooter in the resolution of Who Shot Mr. Burns?, and And Maggie Makes Three retells her arrival as the reason Homer returned to the power plant.

abe_simpson.name: Abraham Simpson
abe_simpson.desc:
Homer's father, known as Grampa, a resident of the Springfield Retirement Castle whose rambling reminiscences trail off before reaching a point. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

He is written as a war veteran and a serial teller of contradictory stories about his own past, a device the writers used to fill in family history whenever a plot required it and to undercut it just as freely.

mona_simpson.name: Mona Simpson
mona_simpson.desc:
Homer's mother, voiced by Glenn Close. Introduced in Mother Simpson in 1995, she is revealed to have gone into hiding after a raid on one of Mr. Burns's laboratories during the 1960s counterculture, leaving Homer to believe she was dead.

She returned in occasional episodes across later seasons before the character was written out in 2008.

herb_powell.name: Herb Powell
herb_powell.desc:
Homer's half-brother, voiced by Danny DeVito. A self-made Detroit car manufacturer, he finds Homer, hands him a design brief and is bankrupted by the resulting car in Oh Brother, Where Art Thou?.

He returned in a later episode in which money from Homer funds an invention that restores his fortune, one of the few Simpsons plots allowed a lasting reversal.

patty_bouvier.name: Patty Bouvier
patty_bouvier.desc:
Marge's chain-smoking twin sister, a clerk at the Springfield Department of Motor Vehicles and one half of a double act built on open contempt for Homer. Voiced by Julie Kavner.

The series established her as a lesbian in a 2005 episode, a development the writers had gestured at for years.

selma_bouvier.name: Selma Bouvier
selma_bouvier.desc:
Marge's twin sister, also voiced by Julie Kavner, distinguished from Patty chiefly by her repeated marriages and her longing for a family of her own.

Her husbands over the years have included Sideshow Bob and Troy McClure, and she eventually adopts a daughter, Ling, from China.

jacqueline_bouvier.name: Jacqueline Bouvier
jacqueline_bouvier.desc: Mother to Marge, Patty and Selma, voiced by Julie Kavner. A frail, disapproving presence who briefly married Abe Simpson before he was displaced by Mr. Burns in Lady Bouvier's Lover.

ling_bouvier.name: Ling Bouvier
ling_bouvier.desc: Selma's adopted daughter, brought back from China in Goo Goo Gai Pan after Selma poses as married in order to satisfy adoption requirements. Her arrival gave Selma the family she had spent fifteen seasons pursuing.

santas_little_helper.name: Santa's Little Helper
santas_little_helper.desc:
The family greyhound, acquired in the first half-hour episode when Homer and Bart find him abandoned at a dog track after he loses his race and his owner disowns him.

His adoption is the emotional resolution of Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire, and he remained a fixture of the household afterwards.

snowball_ii.name: Snowball II
snowball_ii.desc: The Simpsons' black cat, named after a predecessor killed before the series began. The show later ran a joke on its own continuity by killing Snowball II and having Lisa acquire an identical cat, which she renames Snowball II to spare herself the trouble.

ned_flanders.name: Ned Flanders
ned_flanders.desc:
The Simpsons' relentlessly cheerful neighbour, an evangelical Christian, left-hander and proprietor of the Leftorium. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

Originally a minor foil whose only function was to be better at everything than Homer, Ned developed into one of the show's fullest supporting characters, with episodes exploring his faith, his repressed anger and his upbringing by beatnik parents. His speech is marked by nonsense diminutives such as hi-diddly-ho.

maude_flanders.name: Maude Flanders
maude_flanders.desc:
Ned's wife, a mild churchgoing presence voiced by Maggie Roswell. She was killed off in Alone Again, Natura-Diddily in 2000, struck by a volley of T-shirts fired into the stands at a racetrack.

The decision followed Roswell's departure from the show in a pay dispute, and the character was written out rather than recast.

rod_and_todd.name: Rod and Todd Flanders
rod_and_todd.desc:
Ned and Maude's sons, raised on Bible games and a diet of prohibition so complete that Bart finds them baffling. Rod is voiced by Pamela Hayden and Todd by Nancy Cartwright.

The pair serve mainly as a contrast to the Simpson children next door, and occasionally as evidence that Ned's parenting produces something other than serenity.

apu_nahasapeemapetilon.name: Apu Nahasapeemapetilon
apu_nahasapeemapetilon.desc:
Proprietor of the Kwik-E-Mart, a doctorate holder in computer science working long shifts behind a convenience store counter. Voiced by Hank Azaria from the character's introduction until 2020.

Apu received substantial storylines of his own, including an arranged marriage to Manjula and the birth of octuplets. From the 2010s the portrayal drew sustained criticism as a stereotype, examined at length in the 2017 documentary The Problem with Apu, after which Azaria said he would step away from the role.

manjula_nahasapeemapetilon.name: Manjula Nahasapeemapetilon
manjula_nahasapeemapetilon.desc:
Apu's wife, introduced in The Two Mrs. Nahasapeemapetilons, in which an arranged marriage agreed in childhood catches up with him. Voiced by Jan Hooks and later by Tress MacNeille.

Her subsequent storylines include fertility treatment leading to octuplets and a later separation from Apu.

moe_szyslak.name: Moe Szyslak
moe_szyslak.desc:
Bartender and owner of Moe's Tavern, Homer's local. Voiced by Hank Azaria, who has said the voice began as an impression of an actor's gravelly delivery.

Moe is written as the show's bleakest regular, prone to despair, cheating his customers and enduring Bart's prank calls asking for absurd names. Episodes built around him tend to sit at the darker end of the series while remaining a comedy.

barney_gumble.name: Barney Gumble
barney_gumble.desc:
Homer's oldest friend and the tavern's most committed customer, introduced with a belch as his signature. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

The show gave him a genuine arc in 2000, when he stopped drinking and stayed sober for a run of subsequent seasons, and earlier episodes established him as a promising student before Homer introduced him to beer.

dr_hibbert.name: Dr. Julius Hibbert
dr_hibbert.desc:
Springfield's genial family physician, whose habit of chuckling at inappropriate moments is his defining trait. Voiced by Harry Shearer until 2021 and by Kevin Michael Richardson since.

He delivers the town's diagnoses with unhurried good humour regardless of severity, a running joke the show has used since the first seasons.

dr_nick_riviera.name: Dr. Nick Riviera
dr_nick_riviera.desc:
A cut-price physician of dubious qualification, greeting patients with an enthusiastic hello and operating on them with visible improvisation. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

He functions as Hibbert's opposite: where Hibbert is competent and unfeeling, Dr. Nick is warm and dangerous. He was killed off in The Simpsons Movie and reappeared afterwards without explanation.

comic_book_guy.name: Comic Book Guy
comic_book_guy.desc:
Owner of the Android's Dungeon comic shop, a sarcastic, encyclopedic pedant whose verdicts arrive in the form of superlatives. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

The show later gave him the name Jeff Albertson. He is the series' standing caricature of its own most devoted audience, most pointedly in the Poochie episode, where he denounces a cartoon for declining in quality and is told that he is getting it for free.

cletus_spuckler.name: Cletus Spuckler
cletus_spuckler.desc:
Springfield's resident rural caricature, introduced with an on-screen label identifying him as a slack-jawed yokel, and accompanied over the years by an ever-expanding brood of children.

Voiced by Hank Azaria. He and his partner Brandine are used for the show's broadest and most frequently criticised class comedy.

hans_moleman.name: Hans Moleman
hans_moleman.desc:
A tiny, elderly, near-blind man who appears wherever the plot needs someone to be crushed, buried, launched or otherwise destroyed, and who returns unharmed in the following episode. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

His home movie of himself being struck in the groin by a football is the centrepiece of a running joke about American home video contests.

gil_gunderson.name: Gil Gunderson
gil_gunderson.desc:
A perpetually failing salesman introduced in the late 1990s, whose every pitch collapses and who begs for one more chance. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

Writers have described him as modelled on the desperate salesman of Glengarry Glen Ross, and he was introduced as the show's answer to the loss of Phil Hartman's characters.

duffman.name: Duffman
duffman.desc:
The relentlessly enthusiastic mascot of Duff Beer, a caped promotional figure who speaks about himself in the third person and thrusts his hips at every opportunity. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

The show has repeatedly noted that the man inside the costume changes while Duffman himself can never die.

bumblebee_man.name: Bumblebee Man
bumblebee_man.desc:
The star of a Spanish-language slapstick programme on Springfield's Channel Ocho, seen almost exclusively in bee costume being struck by scenery. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

He is a parody of the Mexican comedy character Chapulín Colorado, and the show occasionally shows him off duty speaking normally.

crazy_cat_lady.name: Eleanor Abernathy
crazy_cat_lady.desc:
The Crazy Cat Lady, who communicates by shrieking and hurling cats. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

A later episode gave her the name Eleanor Abernathy and a backstory as a burnt-out doctor and lawyer, retrofitting a joke character with a history.

agnes_skinner.name: Agnes Skinner
agnes_skinner.desc:
Seymour Skinner's domineering mother, who lives with her middle-aged son and undermines him at every opportunity. Voiced by Tress MacNeille.

The relationship is the show's longest-running study in arrested development, and it supplies the emotional stakes of The Principal and the Pauper.

kirk_van_houten.name: Kirk Van Houten
kirk_van_houten.desc:
Milhouse's father, a cracker-factory executive whose divorce from Luann and subsequent decline into bachelorhood formed one of the show's earliest sustained subplots for a secondary character. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

His attempts at reinvention, including a demo tape of a song about his separation, are played as sustained humiliation.

luann_van_houten.name: Luann Van Houten
luann_van_houten.desc: Milhouse's mother, voiced by Maggie Roswell. Her separation from Kirk in A Milhouse Divided leaves Milhouse shuttling between parents, and prompts Homer to reconsider his own marriage.

artie_ziff.name: Artie Ziff
artie_ziff.desc:
Marge's high-school prom date, voiced by Jon Lovitz. Introduced in The Way We Was, he takes Marge to the prom and behaves badly enough that she leaves with Homer instead.

He returns across later seasons as a technology millionaire still pursuing her, each appearance rewriting his fortunes.

professor_frink.name: Professor John Frink
professor_frink.desc:
Springfield's resident scientist, whose inventions solve the problem in the first act and cause a worse one in the second. Voiced by Hank Azaria, who has described the delivery as derived from Jerry Lewis's Nutty Professor.

His speech dissolves into nonsense syllables under stress, and his devices are the show's usual mechanism for introducing implausible technology.

fat_tony.name: Fat Tony
fat_tony.desc:
Head of Springfield's Mafia, voiced by Joe Mantegna since the character's introduction in Bart the Murderer in 1991.

He conducts organised crime with impeccable courtesy, which is the joke: threats are delivered as reasonable business propositions. Mantegna's performance made a one-episode guest role into a recurring fixture of the town.

snake_jailbird.name: Snake Jailbird
snake_jailbird.desc:
Springfield's habitual criminal, who robs the Kwik-E-Mart with a laid-back surfer cadence and is returned to prison at the end of most appearances. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

Running jokes establish him as unexpectedly well educated, and the show frequently has him escape custody between episodes without comment.

kang_and_kodos.name: Kang and Kodos
kang_and_kodos.desc:
Tentacled aliens from Rigel VII who appear in almost every Treehouse of Horror episode, cackling at their own menace. Voiced by Harry Shearer and Dan Castellaneta.

Their best-known appearance impersonates both candidates in a presidential election, a segment the show has returned to as a template in later election years.

springfield.name: Springfield
springfield.desc:
The town the Simpsons live in, whose state is never established. The show has turned that omission into a sustained running joke, cutting away or obscuring the answer whenever a character is about to say it.

Springfield is deliberately generic: it contains a nuclear plant, a gorge, a tyre fire, a monorail for one episode, and whatever geography a given plot requires. The elasticity is the point, letting the writers satirise almost any aspect of American civic life without leaving the setting.

kwik_e_mart.name: Kwik-E-Mart
kwik_e_mart.desc:
Springfield's convenience store, run by Apu, where prices are indefensible, the hot dogs rotate indefinitely and the store is robbed with some regularity.

It is one of the show's fixed comic locations, and was recreated as real, temporary retail outlets in a 2007 promotional campaign for The Simpsons Movie.

shelbyville.name: Shelbyville
shelbyville.desc:
Springfield's neighbouring town and standing rival, founded according to the show's own mythology by a splinter group that left over an irreconcilable disagreement with Springfield's founder.

Lemon of Troy builds an entire episode from the rivalry, sending Bart and his friends across the town line to recover a stolen lemon tree.

seymour_skinner.name: Seymour Skinner
seymour_skinner.desc:
Principal of Springfield Elementary, a former soldier who runs the school as a losing rearguard action against budget cuts, his own mother and Bart Simpson. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

His authority is undermined from every direction: by Superintendent Chalmers above him, by Bart below him, and by Agnes Skinner at home. The 1997 episode The Principal and the Pauper revealed him as an impostor named Armin Tamzarian, a twist the show subsequently declared should be disregarded.

superintendent_chalmers.name: Gary Chalmers
superintendent_chalmers.desc:
Superintendent of Springfield's schools and Skinner's exasperated superior, voiced by Hank Azaria. His bellowed use of Skinner's surname became one of the show's most quoted line readings.

He is written as the one competent adult in the school system, which is precisely why he is always leaving in disgust. His lunch at Skinner's house in 22 Short Films About Springfield later became an internet meme in its own right.

edna_krabappel.name: Edna Krabappel
edna_krabappel.desc:
Bart's fourth-grade teacher, a burnt-out cynic whose mirthless laugh punctuates her assessments of her pupils' futures. Voiced by Marcia Wallace, who won a Primetime Emmy for the role.

Episodes gave her a romance with Skinner and later a marriage to Ned Flanders. After Wallace's death in 2013 the producers retired the character rather than recast her.

milhouse_van_houten.name: Milhouse Van Houten
milhouse_van_houten.desc:
Bart's best friend, a bespectacled, allergic, hopelessly unlucky boy whose devotion to Lisa is never returned. Voiced by Pamela Hayden.

By Matt Groening's account the name comes from Richard Milhous Nixon's middle name. Milhouse absorbs the consequences of Bart's schemes and is the show's most reliable vehicle for humiliation played for sympathy.

nelson_muntz.name: Nelson Muntz
nelson_muntz.desc:
The school bully, identified by a two-syllable derisive laugh delivered at anyone's misfortune. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

Later episodes filled in a home life of poverty and an absent father, and the show has used him for some of its most abrupt shifts from cruelty to pathos, including a brief romance with Lisa.

martin_prince.name: Martin Prince
martin_prince.desc:
The class swot, a precocious, unbearable overachiever who volunteers answers nobody wanted and is beaten up for it. Voiced by Russi Taylor.

He is Lisa's academic rival without her conscience, and the show frequently uses him to show that intelligence alone does not make a sympathetic character.

ralph_wiggum.name: Ralph Wiggum
ralph_wiggum.desc:
Chief Wiggum's son, a classmate of Lisa's whose non-sequiturs are delivered with complete serenity. Voiced by Nancy Cartwright.

Ralph began as a background pupil and grew into one of the show's most quoted characters, largely on the strength of individual lines. I Love Lisa built a whole episode from his misreading of a Valentine's card.

sherri_and_terri.name: Sherri and Terri
sherri_and_terri.desc:
Identical purple-haired twins in Bart's class, voiced by Russi Taylor, who speak in unison to deliver bad news and taunts.

They exist mainly as a chorus, confirming whatever social judgement the school has already reached about Bart.

jimbo_dolph_kearney.name: Jimbo, Dolph and Kearney
jimbo_dolph_kearney.desc:
Springfield's older delinquents, usually seen loitering outside the Kwik-E-Mart or menacing younger children. Voiced variously by Pamela Hayden, Tress MacNeille and Nancy Cartwright.

They outrank Nelson in the school's hierarchy of intimidation, and running jokes establish Kearney as far older than his classmates, with a car, an ex-wife and a son.

groundskeeper_willie.name: Groundskeeper Willie
groundskeeper_willie.desc:
The school's Scottish groundskeeper, introduced in 1990, whose rage is out of all proportion to his position and whose accent the show treats as a punchline in itself. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

He lives in a shack on school grounds, is repeatedly conscripted into whatever menial task the plot needs, and delivers the series' insults about other nationalities with particular relish.

otto_mann.name: Otto Mann
otto_mann.desc:
The school bus driver, a heavy-metal enthusiast of dubious competence and no fixed address. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

Episodes have had him lose his licence, live in the Simpsons' garage and turn out to be the school's least supervised employee, all without endangering his job for long.

springfield_elementary.name: Springfield Elementary School
springfield_elementary.desc:
The Simpson children's school, chronically underfunded, asbestos-lined and staffed by the demoralised. It is the setting for much of the show's satire of American public education, from budget crises to standardised testing.

The institution supplies the show with an entire secondary cast, and the fixed antagonism between Bart and Skinner within it is one of the series' longest-running engines.

mr_burns.name: Charles Montgomery Burns
mr_burns.desc:
Owner of the Springfield Nuclear Power Plant and the show's principal villain, a figure of enormous age and wealth whose cruelty is undercut by his physical frailty. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

Burns cannot remember Homer's name from one episode to the next, a running joke the show has sustained for decades. He has blocked out the sun, run for governor, hunted for sport and been shot by an infant, and the writers have repeatedly used him to satirise concentrated wealth without ever making him competent enough to be genuinely frightening.

waylon_smithers.name: Waylon Smithers
waylon_smithers.desc:
Mr. Burns's executive assistant, whose devotion to his employer is total and unreciprocated. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

Smithers's love for Burns was played for years as innuendo before later seasons made it explicit and gave him relationships and storylines of his own. He is also the one person at the plant who knows how it works.

lenny_leonard.name: Lenny Leonard
lenny_leonard.desc:
One of Homer's two closest colleagues at the power plant and a regular at Moe's. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

Lenny and Carl function as a near-inseparable pair, and the show has run a long joke about how little any character actually knows about them, occasionally revealing an unexpected qualification or a wound in one line and never mentioning it again.

carl_carlson.name: Carl Carlson
carl_carlson.desc:
Homer's colleague at the plant, the more sardonic half of the Lenny and Carl pairing, and the holder of a master's degree in nuclear physics that never affects his position.

Voiced by Hank Azaria until 2020, when the producers recast the role with Alex Désert as part of a decision to stop having white actors voice non-white characters.

frank_grimes.name: Frank Grimes
frank_grimes.desc:
A new employee at the power plant in Homer's Enemy, a man who worked for everything he has and is destroyed by proximity to a colleague who has more and earned none of it.

He is the show's most direct experiment in importing a realistic person into Springfield, and the episode ends with his death by electrocution while imitating Homer. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

hank_scorpio.name: Hank Scorpio
hank_scorpio.desc:
The proprietor of Globex Corporation in You Only Move Twice, voiced by Albert Brooks. An exemplary, warm and genuinely supportive employer who is also a Bond-style supervillain seizing the East Coast.

The joke is entirely in the collision: he treats Homer better than anyone ever has while flamethrowing government agents in the background.

springfield_nuclear_plant.name: Springfield Nuclear Power Plant
springfield_nuclear_plant.desc:
Mr. Burns's plant and Homer's workplace, run with a disregard for safety that supplies the show with mutations, leaks and inspection farces.

It anchors the series' satire of corporate negligence: cooling towers loom over the town, waste is disposed of wherever is convenient, and the man responsible for safety sleeps at his desk.

moes_tavern.name: Moe's Tavern
moes_tavern.desc:
The dive bar where Homer, Barney, Lenny and Carl drink, and the target of Bart's prank calls. Its telephone, its grimy interior and its handful of regulars make it the show's second home after the Simpson house.

It has been remodelled, franchised and burned in various episodes, and always returns exactly as it was.

blinky.name: Blinky
blinky.desc:
The three-eyed orange fish caught in the river beside the power plant in Two Cars in Every Garage and Three Eyes on Every Fish.

Blinky became the show's shorthand for nuclear contamination, appearing in later episodes and in merchandising as a symbol of what the plant does to Springfield.

duff_beer.name: Duff Beer
duff_beer.desc:
Springfield's ubiquitous lager, Homer's drink of choice and the sponsor of most local entertainment. The show uses it for satire of brewing and advertising, notably in an episode revealing that Duff, Duff Lite and Duff Dry all come from a single pipe.

The brand's mascot Duffman and its brewery tour have both anchored episodes.

krusty_the_clown.name: Krusty the Clown
krusty_the_clown.desc:
Host of Springfield's children's television programme, a chain-smoking, gambling-addicted, thrice-divorced entertainer who despises his audience and sells them anything. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

Krusty is the show's vehicle for satire of the television industry itself: merchandising, licensing, cancellation and the gulf between a performer's on-screen persona and his life. Like Father, Like Clown established him as the estranged son of a rabbi, with Jackie Mason guest-starring as his father.

sideshow_bob.name: Sideshow Bob
sideshow_bob.desc:
Robert Underdunk Terwilliger, Krusty's former sidekick turned recurring criminal, voiced by Kelsey Grammer, who has won a Primetime Emmy for the role.

Introduced as a mute stooge in Krusty Gets Busted, he framed Krusty for armed robbery and was exposed by Bart, beginning a feud that has run for decades. Bob is cultured, articulate and murderous, and his schemes are undone by his own refinement as reliably as by Bart.

sideshow_mel.name: Sideshow Mel
sideshow_mel.desc:
Krusty's replacement sidekick after Bob's imprisonment, distinguished by a bone through his hair and a booming theatrical delivery. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

Off air he speaks with the same Shakespearean formality, and the show occasionally reveals his private life to be more dignified than his employer's.

itchy_and_scratchy.name: Itchy and Scratchy
itchy_and_scratchy.desc:
The cartoon-within-the-cartoon shown on Krusty's programme, in which a mouse dismembers a cat in escalating ways.

It lets the show satirise the debate about violence in children's television from inside a children's cartoon, most explicitly in the episode where Marge campaigns to have it toned down and the resulting sanitised version proves unwatchable. The Itchy and Scratchy studio also gave the writers a stage for satire of their own industry.

poochie.name: Poochie
poochie.desc:
A surfing, rapping dog added to Itchy and Scratchy by network executives in The Itchy and Scratchy and Poochie Show, and killed off at the end of his first appearance.

Poochie is the show's most direct attack on network note-giving and on demands to freshen a long-running series, and his name has since been used generally for an unwanted character added to revive a franchise. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

kent_brockman.name: Kent Brockman
kent_brockman.desc:
Anchor of Channel 6 news, a vain and credulous broadcaster who reports whatever will hold an audience and switches allegiance the instant power shifts. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

His line welcoming new insect overlords, delivered in Deep Space Homer after misreading pictures from a space shuttle, became a widely reused template for capitulation jokes far beyond the show.

troy_mcclure.name: Troy McClure
troy_mcclure.desc:
A washed-up actor who introduces himself by listing films nobody has seen, and who narrates the educational reels, infomercials and telethons the plot requires. Voiced by Phil Hartman.

After Hartman's death in 1998 the producers retired the character rather than recast him, and his largest role was as the star of a stage musical of Planet of the Apes, in an episode built entirely around him.

lionel_hutz.name: Lionel Hutz
lionel_hutz.desc:
Springfield's ambulance-chasing attorney, operating from a shopping-mall office that also offers shoe repair. Voiced by Phil Hartman.

Hutz loses cases through spectacular incompetence and admits it cheerfully, and the show used him whenever a plot needed the legal system rendered absurd. Like Troy McClure, he was retired after Hartman's death.

rainier_wolfcastle.name: Rainier Wolfcastle
rainier_wolfcastle.desc:
An Austrian-accented action star, best known in Springfield for playing the violent hero McBain. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

The character is a broad parody of Arnold Schwarzenegger's screen persona, and his McBain films appear as short interstitial parodies that the writers occasionally assembled into a continuous story.

radioactive_man.name: Radioactive Man
radioactive_man.desc:
The superhero comic Bart and Milhouse collect, complete with a sidekick, Fallout Boy, and an unwieldy publication history parodying real comics continuity.

A 1995 episode brings a film adaptation to Springfield, with Milhouse cast as Fallout Boy, and satirises location shooting and child stardom. The comic was also published for real as a tie-in series.

bleeding_gums_murphy.name: Bleeding Gums Murphy
bleeding_gums_murphy.desc:
A jazz saxophonist Lisa meets on a bridge in the show's first season, and the only Springfield adult who takes her seriously as a musician. Voiced by Ron Taylor.

His death in the 1995 episode Round Springfield gave Lisa the series' most sustained treatment of grief, and established a pattern of using her musical life for its rare unironic material.

be_sharps.name: The Be Sharps
be_sharps.desc:
The barbershop quartet Homer forms with Skinner, Apu and Barney in Homer's Barbershop Quartet, whose rise and collapse parodies the Beatles' career in a single episode.

The episode ends with the group reunited on a rooftop, with George Harrison appearing as himself to comment on the scene.

chief_wiggum.name: Clancy Wiggum
chief_wiggum.desc:
Springfield's chief of police, incompetent, corruptible and usually eating. Voiced by Hank Azaria.

Wiggum's department solves crimes by accident when it solves them at all, which allows the show to run plots that would otherwise be ended by functioning law enforcement. He is Ralph's father, and the two share a warmth that is among the show's more genuine parent-child relationships.

mayor_quimby.name: Joe Quimby
mayor_quimby.desc:
Springfield's mayor, a Kennedy-accented machine politician whose administration runs on graft, patronage and settled lawsuits. Voiced by Dan Castellaneta.

He is the show's standing joke about American local government: he reverses policy under any pressure, and his sash and his nephews appear in whatever scheme is currently emptying the town treasury.

reverend_lovejoy.name: Timothy Lovejoy
reverend_lovejoy.desc:
Minister of the First Church of Springfield, whose pastoral enthusiasm was worn away by Ned Flanders's constant telephone calls. Voiced by Harry Shearer.

He preaches with audible boredom and refers parishioners to the church's answering machine. In Marge We Trust gives him a model railway as his real devotion and sends him back to the job with something like conviction. The show uses him to satirise institutional religion while treating belief itself more gently.

helen_lovejoy.name: Helen Lovejoy
helen_lovejoy.desc:
The minister's wife and Springfield's chief gossip, whose appeal that somebody think of the children became one of the show's most durable catchphrases. Voiced by Maggie Roswell.

She is the town's engine of moral panic, and the phrase has passed into general use as shorthand for an appeal to sentiment in place of an argument.

first_church_of_springfield.name: First Church of Springfield
first_church_of_springfield.desc:
The town's church, attended by most of the cast on Sundays and used by the show as a fixed setting for satire of American religious life.

Its congregation includes Ned Flanders in the front pew and Homer asleep beside him, and episodes set there have covered fundraising, schism, competing faiths and the church burning down.

stonecutters.name: The Stonecutters
stonecutters.desc:
A secret society introduced in Homer the Great, whose membership includes most of Springfield's men and whose meetings consist mainly of drinking and a song listing their hidden powers.

The episode satirises fraternal orders and conspiracy theory at once: the society really does control everything, and does nothing with it. Homer is elevated to Chosen One on the strength of a birthmark and immediately ruins the order.

matt_groening.name: Matt Groening
matt_groening.desc:
Cartoonist and creator of The Simpsons. He was already known for the alternative weekly comic strip Life in Hell when James L. Brooks approached him about producing animated shorts for The Tracey Ullman Show.

By Groening's own account he devised the Simpson family in the lobby before the meeting, rather than license his existing characters, and named them after members of his own family: his parents Homer and Margaret and his sisters Lisa and Maggie, with Bart an anagram of brat. He later co-created Futurama and Disenchantment.

james_l_brooks.name: James L. Brooks
james_l_brooks.desc:
Film and television producer whose company Gracie Films produced The Simpsons, and the figure whose standing made the series possible.

Already an established writer-producer from The Mary Tyler Moore Show and Taxi and an Academy Award winner for Terms of Endearment, he secured the show an unusual degree of freedom from network interference. His insistence on emotional stakes underneath the jokes shaped the series' willingness to end episodes on sincerity.

sam_simon.name: Sam Simon
sam_simon.desc:
Writer and producer credited alongside Groening and Brooks with developing The Simpsons from shorts into a half-hour series. He assembled and ran the original writing staff and established the show's writers' room.

He left after the fourth season following disagreements with Groening, retaining an executive producer credit and a share of the show's revenue thereafter. He gave much of that income to animal welfare and other charities before his death in 2015.

al_jean.name: Al Jean
al_jean.desc:
Writer and producer who joined the show at its start, ran it with Mike Reiss during its third and fourth seasons, and returned as showrunner from the thirteenth season onwards.

His second tenure is by far the longest in the show's history, making him the person most responsible for the series in its modern form. He and Reiss also created The Critic.

mike_reiss.name: Mike Reiss
mike_reiss.desc:
Writer and producer, Al Jean's longstanding writing partner, and co-showrunner of the third and fourth seasons, a period widely regarded as the show's creative peak.

He remained connected to the series as a consultant for decades afterwards, and co-created The Critic with Jean.

david_mirkin.name: David Mirkin
david_mirkin.desc:
Showrunner for the fifth and sixth seasons, arriving from Get a Life with a taste for surrealism that pushed the series further from domestic realism.

His tenure produced Deep Space Homer, which he wrote and which some staff argued at the time went too far in sending Homer into orbit, and the first part of Who Shot Mr. Burns? was developed under his watch as an end-of-season cliffhanger.

bill_oakley.name: Bill Oakley
bill_oakley.desc:
Writer and, with Josh Weinstein, showrunner of the seventh and eighth seasons. The pair favoured episodes grounded in character and in Springfield's own history, and deliberately gave secondary characters their own showcases.

Oakley has since become a widely followed commentator on the show's history and on the food industry.

josh_weinstein.name: Josh Weinstein
josh_weinstein.desc:
Writer and co-showrunner with Bill Oakley of the seventh and eighth seasons. The two had written together since school and joined the staff in the early 1990s.

Their run included Homer's Enemy, 22 Short Films About Springfield and the resolution of the Who Shot Mr. Burns? cliffhanger.

mike_scully.name: Mike Scully
mike_scully.desc:
Showrunner from the ninth to the twelfth seasons. His tenure moved the show towards broader, faster and more plot-driven comedy, and is the period most often cited in arguments about a decline in quality.

It also produced Behind the Laughter, an Emmy-winning parody of music documentaries that turned the show's own history into its subject.

matt_selman.name: Matt Selman
matt_selman.desc:
Writer and executive producer who joined in the late 1990s and has since shared showrunning duties with Al Jean, taking the lead on a portion of episodes in recent seasons.

He was among the writers credited on The Simpsons Movie.

conan_obrien.name: Conan O'Brien
conan_obrien.desc:
Writer on the show in the early 1990s, before he was known as a performer. He wrote Marge vs. the Monorail and Homer Goes to College, both built on a heightened absurdity that influenced the writing around him.

He left in 1993 to host Late Night on NBC, a move that at the time meant giving up a secure job for an untested one.

george_meyer.name: George Meyer
george_meyer.desc:
Writer and producer, on the staff from the first season and for many years afterwards. Much of his contribution came through rewriting in the room rather than through credited scripts.

Colleagues have repeatedly credited him with shaping the show's comic voice more than anyone else, an assessment set out at length in a 2000 New Yorker profile.

john_swartzwelder.name: John Swartzwelder
john_swartzwelder.desc:
The show's most prolific writer, credited with more episodes than anyone else, and famous among colleagues for his reclusiveness and his refusal to give interviews for decades.

His scripts favour absurd escalation and Homer at his most purely appetitive, and include Homer at the Bat, You Only Move Twice and Homer's Enemy. He has since self-published a series of comic novels.

jon_vitti.name: Jon Vitti
jon_vitti.desc:
Writer on the original staff, responsible for many of the early episodes that established the characters, including Bart the Genius and Cape Feare.

His scripts are noted for tight construction and for finding the emotional core of a character early in the show's run, when the family were still being defined.

david_x_cohen.name: David X. Cohen
david_x_cohen.desc:
Writer on the show in the mid-1990s, credited on early episodes as David S. Cohen. He wrote Lisa the Vegetarian, the episode that changed Lisa's diet permanently.

He went on to develop Futurama with Matt Groening and served as its showrunner, bringing a mathematics and computer science background to its jokes.

greg_daniels.name: Greg Daniels
greg_daniels.desc:
Writer on the show in the mid-1990s, whose scripts include Lisa's Wedding and Bart Sells His Soul.

He later co-created King of the Hill with Mike Judge and developed the American version of The Office, carrying the character-first approach of his Simpsons work into live action.

ken_keeler.name: Ken Keeler
ken_keeler.desc:
Writer and producer who joined in the mid-1990s and wrote The Principal and the Pauper, one of the most contested episodes in the show's history. He has publicly defended the episode against its critics.

He later wrote and produced for Futurama, where an episode of his required a mathematical proof he devised for the purpose.

jay_kogen.name: Jay Kogen
jay_kogen.desc:
Writer on the early seasons, working as a team with Wallace Wolodarsky. Their credits include Krusty Gets Busted and Last Exit to Springfield.

The pair came to the show from Brooks's circle and were among the writers who established the early template of an emotional turn beneath the jokes.

wallace_wolodarsky.name: Wallace Wolodarsky
wallace_wolodarsky.desc:
Writer on the early seasons, partnered with Jay Kogen on scripts including Last Exit to Springfield, frequently named in critics' polls as the series' best episode.

He later moved into directing and screenwriting for film.

brad_bird.name: Brad Bird
brad_bird.desc:
Animator and director who served as an executive consultant on the early seasons, supervising animation and directing episodes including Krusty Gets Busted.

He also directed the video for Do the Bartman. He went on to direct The Iron Giant, The Incredibles and Ratatouille.

david_silverman.name: David Silverman
david_silverman.desc:
Animator and director involved since the Tracey Ullman shorts, and one of the people most responsible for how the characters actually move.

He directed many episodes across the early seasons, served as director of animation, and directed The Simpsons Movie in 2007.

rich_moore.name: Rich Moore
rich_moore.desc:
Director on the early seasons, whose episodes include Marge vs. the Monorail.

He later directed Wreck-It Ralph and co-directed Zootopia for Disney, having learned large-scale comic staging on a show that had to build a new set of gags every week.

richard_sakai.name: Richard Sakai
richard_sakai.desc:
Producer and long-serving executive at Gracie Films, credited as a producer on The Simpsons from its earliest seasons and on The Simpsons Movie.

He worked with James L. Brooks across television and film, and represents the production company's continuity behind the changing writing staff.

dan_castellaneta.name: Dan Castellaneta
dan_castellaneta.desc:
The voice of Homer Simpson, and of Grampa, Krusty, Barney, Groundskeeper Willie, Mayor Quimby and many others. He came to the shorts from The Tracey Ullman Show's repertory cast.

He has won several Primetime Emmys for the role. He has said Homer's voice began as an impression of Walter Matthau before settling into something he could sustain, and that d'oh derives from a shortened version of an exasperated cry used by the comic actor James Finlayson.

julie_kavner.name: Julie Kavner
julie_kavner.desc:
The voice of Marge Simpson and of her sisters Patty and Selma and their mother Jacqueline. Like Castellaneta she was a member of the Tracey Ullman Show cast, having previously been known for Rhoda.

She has won a Primetime Emmy for the role, and she is unusual among the cast in declining most publicity and rarely performing her characters in public.

nancy_cartwright.name: Nancy Cartwright
nancy_cartwright.desc:
The voice of Bart Simpson, and also of Nelson, Ralph Wiggum and Todd Flanders. She has said she auditioned for Lisa and asked to read for Bart instead after seeing the character description.

She has won a Primetime Emmy for the role and wrote a memoir about playing the character.

yeardley_smith.name: Yeardley Smith
yeardley_smith.desc:
The voice of Lisa Simpson, and the only member of the principal cast who regularly voices a single character.

Her natural speaking voice is close to Lisa's, which she has said made the audition unusual. She has won a Primetime Emmy for the role.

hank_azaria.name: Hank Azaria
hank_azaria.desc:
Voice of Moe, Chief Wiggum, Comic Book Guy, Professor Frink, Snake, Duffman and, for three decades, Apu. He joined during the first season, brought in to fill in on Moe, and stayed.

He has won several Primetime Emmys for his work on the show. In 2020 he said he would stop voicing Apu, following years of criticism of the portrayal and public reflection on his own part in it.

harry_shearer.name: Harry Shearer
harry_shearer.desc:
Voice of Mr. Burns, Smithers, Ned Flanders, Principal Skinner, Kent Brockman, Otto, Lenny and Reverend Lovejoy, among others. He came to the show from Saturday Night Live and This Is Spinal Tap.

He has been the cast's most public critic of the show's business arrangements, and briefly left in 2015 during a contract dispute before returning. He gave up voicing Dr. Hibbert in 2021 as part of the show's recasting of non-white characters.

marcia_wallace.name: Marcia Wallace
marcia_wallace.desc:
The voice of Edna Krabappel, a role she played from the first season until her death in 2013, and for which she won a Primetime Emmy.

She was already known as the receptionist on The Bob Newhart Show. After her death the producers retired Mrs. Krabappel, and the character's absence was acknowledged on screen.

phil_hartman.name: Phil Hartman
phil_hartman.desc:
Guest voice of Troy McClure and Lionel Hutz across dozens of episodes, and among the most frequently used performers outside the regular cast.

He was killed in 1998. Producers have said that plans involving his characters, including a proposed Troy McClure film, were abandoned, and both roles were retired rather than recast.

tress_macneille.name: Tress MacNeille
tress_macneille.desc:
A supporting cast member since the early 1990s, voicing Agnes Skinner, Dolph, the Crazy Cat Lady, Lindsey Naegle and many one-episode parts.

She supplies a large share of the show's female incidental characters, and has a long parallel career in American animation.

pamela_hayden.name: Pamela Hayden
pamela_hayden.desc:
Voice of Milhouse Van Houten, Jimbo Jones and Rod Flanders, among other recurring children, from the show's early seasons.

Her work covers much of the school's population, and Milhouse in particular has carried a substantial share of episodes.

maggie_roswell.name: Maggie Roswell
maggie_roswell.desc:
Voice of Maude Flanders, Helen Lovejoy and Elizabeth Hoover. She left the show in 1999 in a dispute over pay and travel costs, and Maude Flanders was killed off shortly afterwards.

Roswell returned to the series a few years later, resuming her other characters.

russi_taylor.name: Russi Taylor
russi_taylor.desc:
Voice of Martin Prince, Sherri and Terri, and Üter, from the show's early seasons until her death in 2019.

She was also the long-serving voice of Minnie Mouse for Disney, and was married to Wayne Allwine, the voice of Mickey Mouse.

kelsey_grammer.name: Kelsey Grammer
kelsey_grammer.desc:
The voice of Sideshow Bob since 1990, a recurring role he has played alongside his live-action career on Cheers and Frasier.

He has won a Primetime Emmy for the performance, and the character's operatic diction and singing voice are built directly on his stage training.

joe_mantegna.name: Joe Mantegna
joe_mantegna.desc:
The voice of Fat Tony since 1991, one of the show's longest-serving recurring guest performers.

A Tony Award winner for Glengarry Glen Ross, he plays the mob boss with a courtesy that makes the threats funnier, and the character has outlasted most one-episode guest creations by decades.

kevin_michael_richardson.name: Kevin Michael Richardson
kevin_michael_richardson.desc:
Voice actor who took over Dr. Hibbert in 2021, after the producers decided that white actors would no longer voice non-white characters.

He had already appeared on the show in other roles, and has an extensive career across American animation.

alex_desert.name: Alex Désert
alex_desert.desc:
Actor who took over the voice of Carl Carlson in 2020 under the same recasting decision, replacing Hank Azaria in the role.

He was already known for live-action television work and for playing in the ska band Hepcat.

ep_roasting_open_fire.name: Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire
ep_roasting_open_fire.desc:
The first half-hour episode, broadcast on 17 December 1989. Homer, denied a Christmas bonus, takes a job as a shopping-mall Santa, gambles his wages on a greyhound and comes home with the losing dog instead of presents.

The series' producers have said it was not intended to launch the show, and was moved forward when animation problems delayed the episode originally planned as the premiere. Its ending, in which the family accept the dog as their Christmas, set the pattern of closing on sentiment after half an hour of failure.

ep_bart_genius.name: Bart the Genius
ep_bart_genius.desc:
Broadcast in January 1990, the second episode broadcast and the first to open with the full title sequence including the chalkboard and couch gags.

Bart swaps his test paper with Martin's and is transferred to a school for gifted children, where he is exposed. Written by Jon Vitti, it established the recurring structure of Bart's deception collapsing into an apology to Homer.

ep_krusty_gets_busted.name: Krusty Gets Busted
ep_krusty_gets_busted.desc:
First broadcast in April 1990. Krusty is arrested for an armed robbery at the Kwik-E-Mart, and Bart and Lisa prove he was framed by his own sidekick.

Written by Jay Kogen and Wallace Wolodarsky and directed by Brad Bird, it introduced Sideshow Bob as a speaking character and began the show's longest-running antagonism.

ep_treehouse_1.name: Treehouse of Horror
ep_treehouse_1.desc:
The first Halloween anthology episode, broadcast in October 1990, presenting three horror segments outside the show's continuity, including an adaptation of Edgar Allan Poe's The Raven narrated by James Earl Jones.

Its framing device has the children telling ghost stories in the treehouse, and its success established an annual tradition that has continued ever since.

ep_bart_gets_an_f.name: Bart Gets an F
ep_bart_gets_an_f.desc:
Broadcast on 11 October 1990 as the second season premiere, and widely reported as the most-watched episode in the show's history.

Bart, facing being held back a year, studies desperately and still fails, then weeps when told his answer showed real learning. The episode aired at the height of the show's first wave of popularity and of the debate about Bart as a role model.

ep_bart_daredevil.name: Bart the Daredevil
ep_bart_daredevil.desc:
Broadcast in December 1990. Bart resolves to jump Springfield Gorge on a skateboard; Homer, trying to stop him, ends up going over the edge himself.

The long, brutally protracted fall down the rock face is one of the show's best-remembered visual sequences, and the writers have described building the gag around the audience's expectation that it would end sooner.

ep_the_way_we_was.name: The Way We Was
ep_the_way_we_was.desc:
Broadcast in January 1991. A broken television prompts Homer and Marge to tell the children how they met in high school detention in 1974, and how Marge left the prom with Homer after her date, Artie Ziff, behaved badly.

It was the show's first extended flashback and the template for a long series of episodes filling in the family's past.

ep_lisas_substitute.name: Lisa's Substitute
ep_lisas_substitute.desc:
Broadcast in April 1991. A substitute teacher, Mr. Bergstrom, gives Lisa the intellectual attention her family cannot, and then leaves; his parting note tells her that she is who she is.

Dustin Hoffman voiced Bergstrom under the pseudonym Sam Etic. The episode is frequently cited as the point at which the series proved it could carry genuine emotional weight.

ep_stark_raving_dad.name: Stark Raving Dad
ep_stark_raving_dad.desc:
The third season premiere, broadcast in September 1991. Homer is committed to a mental institution, where he meets a large white man who believes he is Michael Jackson.

Jackson voiced the character under the pseudonym John Jay Smith, with a soundalike performing the singing. In 2019, following the documentary Leaving Neverland, the producers withdrew the episode from circulation and it was removed from streaming and future releases.

ep_flaming_moes.name: Flaming Moe's
ep_flaming_moes.desc:
Broadcast in November 1991. Moe steals Homer's cocktail recipe, renames it after himself and turns his failing bar into the most fashionable place in Springfield.

Aerosmith appear as themselves, among the first bands to guest on the show, and the episode includes a parody of the Cheers theme sung over the bar's transformation.

ep_homer_at_the_bat.name: Homer at the Bat
ep_homer_at_the_bat.desc:
Broadcast on 20 February 1992. Mr. Burns bets on the plant softball team and hires nine Major League players as ringers, all of whom are eliminated by escalating misfortune before the final.

Written by John Swartzwelder, it was the show's most ambitious guest booking to that point, and staff have described the difficulty of recording so many athletes. It aired opposite The Cosby Show and drew a large audience.

ep_kamp_krusty.name: Kamp Krusty
ep_kamp_krusty.desc:
The fourth season premiere, broadcast in September 1992. Bart and Lisa are sent to a summer camp licensed in Krusty's name and run as a labour operation, and Bart leads a revolt.

The premise was originally considered for a feature film before being made as an episode, and it opens the season most often named as the show's strongest.

ep_streetcar_named_marge.name: A Streetcar Named Marge
ep_streetcar_named_marge.desc:
Broadcast in October 1992. Marge is cast as Blanche DuBois in a musical version of A Streetcar Named Desire, and channels her resentment of Homer into the part.

A subplot places Maggie in a nursery styled after The Great Escape. A song in the episode describing New Orleans drew complaints from the city, and the show responded with an on-screen apology in the following episode's chalkboard gag.

ep_mr_plow.name: Mr. Plow
ep_mr_plow.desc:
Broadcast in November 1992. Homer buys a snowplough and builds a successful business on the back of a cheap late-night advertisement, until Barney sets up in competition with a better jingle.

The episode's rival advertising jingles are among the show's most quoted songs, and Adam West appears as himself.

ep_marge_vs_monorail.name: Marge vs. the Monorail
ep_marge_vs_monorail.desc:
Broadcast in January 1993. A confidence man arrives in Springfield and sells the town a monorail with a musical number; Marge alone doubts it, and Homer is made the driver.

Written by Conan O'Brien and directed by Rich Moore, with Leonard Nimoy guest-starring as himself, it is the clearest early example of the show abandoning domestic realism for pure absurdity, and is frequently placed at the top of best-episode lists.

ep_last_exit_springfield.name: Last Exit to Springfield
ep_last_exit_springfield.desc:
Broadcast in March 1993. Homer accidentally becomes head of the plant's union in a dispute over the dental plan, and Burns's attempt to break the strike collapses.

Written by Jay Kogen and Wallace Wolodarsky, it is among the episodes most often named the series' best in critics' polls. It sustains an unusually dense run of parodies, including The Godfather, Batman and Citizen Kane.

ep_homers_barbershop_quartet.name: Homer's Barbershop Quartet
ep_homers_barbershop_quartet.desc:
The fifth season premiere, broadcast in September 1993. A flea-market record prompts Homer to explain that he was once in a chart-topping barbershop quartet, the Be Sharps, whose career follows the Beatles' beat for beat.

George Harrison appears as himself, and the episode ends with the group reuniting on a rooftop.

ep_cape_feare.name: Cape Feare
ep_cape_feare.desc:
Broadcast in October 1993. Sideshow Bob is paroled and pursues the family into witness protection, in a sustained parody of Cape Fear scored with Bernard Herrmann's music.

Written by Jon Vitti, it contains the sequence in which Bob repeatedly steps on rakes, a gag the staff have said was extended far beyond its natural length specifically to fill time, and which became one of the show's most discussed jokes.

ep_rosebud.name: Rosebud
ep_rosebud.desc:
Broadcast in October 1993. Mr. Burns is shown to have lost a childhood teddy bear named Bobo, which has passed through history to reach Maggie, and he will do anything to recover it.

Built on Citizen Kane, it is the fullest account of Burns's early life the show has given, and ends with him choosing to leave the bear with Maggie for as long as his conscience holds.

ep_springfield_gambling.name: $pringfield
ep_springfield_gambling.desc:
Broadcast in December 1993. Springfield legalises gambling to revive its economy, Burns opens a casino, Homer becomes a dealer and Marge develops a compulsion.

Gerry Cooney and Robert Goulet appear as themselves. The episode paired the town-wide satire with one of the show's more serious treatments of addiction inside Marge's storyline.

ep_deep_space_homer.name: Deep Space Homer
ep_deep_space_homer.desc:
Broadcast in February 1994. NASA, worried about falling ratings for launches, recruits an ordinary person and selects Homer, who destroys an ant farm in orbit and returns as a hero alongside an inanimate carbon rod.

Written by David Mirkin and featuring Buzz Aldrin as himself, it drew objections from some staff at the time for pushing the premise too far. Kent Brockman's misreading of the ants on camera became one of the show's most quoted moments.

ep_treehouse_v.name: Treehouse of Horror V
ep_treehouse_v.desc:
Broadcast in October 1994, containing The Shinning, a compressed parody of The Shining in which the power is cut off at the plant's lodge and Homer loses his mind without television or beer.

Its other segments cover time travel through a toaster and a school that serves its pupils for lunch. It is generally considered the strongest of the Halloween anthologies.

ep_homer_the_great.name: Homer the Great
ep_homer_the_great.desc:
Broadcast in January 1995. Homer discovers that Lenny and Carl belong to the Stonecutters, an ancient order controlling everything in Springfield, and is revealed by a birthmark to be their Chosen One.

The episode's song listing the society's secret powers is among the show's best-known musical numbers, and the plot resolves by having Homer destroy the order through sheer earnestness.

ep_and_maggie_makes_three.name: And Maggie Makes Three
ep_and_maggie_makes_three.desc:
Broadcast in January 1995. Asked why there are no photographs of Maggie in the family album, Homer explains that he had left the power plant for his dream job at a bowling alley and had to beg for his old post back when Marge became pregnant.

The episode ends on the plaque Burns hung over his desk to demoralise him, which Homer has covered with pictures of Maggie so that it reads differently.

ep_lisas_wedding.name: Lisa's Wedding
ep_lisas_wedding.desc:
Broadcast in March 1995. A fortune teller shows Lisa her future in 2010, engaged to an urbane English student who cannot tolerate her family.

Written by Greg Daniels, it won a Primetime Emmy and was the show's first flash-forward, establishing a format the series has returned to repeatedly. Its predictions of future technology have been picked over by viewers ever since.

ep_lemon_of_troy.name: Lemon of Troy
ep_lemon_of_troy.desc:
Broadcast in May 1995. Shelbyville children steal Springfield's beloved lemon tree, and Bart leads an expedition across the town line to take it back.

The episode is built entirely on the rivalry between the two towns, and includes the founding myth in which the settlements split over an irreconcilable disagreement between their founders.

ep_who_shot_mr_burns.name: Who Shot Mr. Burns?
ep_who_shot_mr_burns.desc:
A two-part story: the first part closed the sixth season in May 1995 with Burns shot and dying after blocking out Springfield's sun, and the second opened the seventh in September 1995 with the culprit revealed as Maggie.

Written in its first part by Bill Oakley and Josh Weinstein, it was the show's only true season cliffhanger, accompanied by a competition inviting viewers to name the shooter, and it seeded suspects across the whole town.

ep_bart_sells_his_soul.name: Bart Sells His Soul
ep_bart_sells_his_soul.desc:
Broadcast in October 1995. Bart sells Milhouse a piece of paper with the word soul written on it for five dollars, then finds himself unable to laugh, breathe on glass or be noticed by animals.

Written by Greg Daniels, it is one of the show's most direct treatments of belief, and refuses to say whether anything supernatural has happened.

ep_lisa_the_vegetarian.name: Lisa the Vegetarian
ep_lisa_the_vegetarian.desc:
Broadcast in October 1995. After meeting a lamb at a petting zoo, Lisa stops eating meat and is mocked for it, before Apu and guest stars Paul and Linda McCartney persuade her that she need not force the change on anyone else.

Written by David X. Cohen. The McCartneys agreed to appear on the condition that Lisa remain a vegetarian permanently, and the show has kept to it.

ep_mother_simpson.name: Mother Simpson
ep_mother_simpson.desc:
Broadcast in November 1995. Homer fakes his own death to avoid work and discovers that his mother, whom he believed dead, has been in hiding since a raid on one of Burns's laboratories in the 1960s.

Glenn Close first voiced Mona here. The episode ends without music, on Homer sitting alone on the bonnet of his car watching the stars after she is forced to leave again.

ep_22_short_films.name: 22 Short Films About Springfield
ep_22_short_films.desc:
Broadcast in April 1996. An anthology of brief, loosely linked vignettes following the town's secondary characters through a single day, prompted by Bart and Milhouse wondering what everyone else does.

Its segment in which Skinner passes off fast food as a home-cooked lunch to Superintendent Chalmers became, two decades later, one of the internet's most reworked pieces of source material.

ep_you_only_move_twice.name: You Only Move Twice
ep_you_only_move_twice.desc:
Broadcast in November 1996. Homer takes a job with the Globex Corporation and moves the family to a planned community, working for the most supportive employer he has ever had, who is also a supervillain.

Written by John Swartzwelder, with Albert Brooks as Hank Scorpio. The rest of the family's misery in the new town forces a return to Springfield, and Homer never grasps what his employer actually does.

ep_el_viaje_misterioso.name: El Viaje Misterioso de Nuestro Jomer
ep_el_viaje_misterioso.desc:
Broadcast in January 1997. Homer eats an extremely hot chilli pepper at a town cook-off and experiences an extended hallucination guided by a talking coyote, voiced by Johnny Cash.

The sequence's stylised animation is unlike anything else in the series, and the episode returns Homer to a sober question about whether Marge is his soulmate.

ep_homers_phobia.name: Homer's Phobia
ep_homers_phobia.desc:
Broadcast in February 1997. The family befriend John, a collector of kitsch voiced by John Waters, and Homer turns hostile when he learns John is gay, then fears Bart will be influenced.

The episode was reportedly challenged by the network's standards department before a change of personnel let it through. It won a Primetime Emmy and a GLAAD award, and is regularly cited as a turning point in mainstream television's treatment of the subject.

ep_homers_enemy.name: Homer's Enemy
ep_homers_enemy.desc:
Broadcast in May 1997. Frank Grimes, a man who has worked for everything he has, joins the plant and is driven to a fatal breakdown by the fact that Homer has more and deserves none of it.

Written by John Swartzwelder, the episode was conceived by the showrunners as a test of what would happen if a realistic person entered Springfield. It remains one of the series' most argued-over episodes for how bleakly it answers the question.

ep_principal_and_pauper.name: The Principal and the Pauper
ep_principal_and_pauper.desc:
Broadcast in September 1997. Principal Skinner is revealed to be Armin Tamzarian, a street kid who assumed the identity of a soldier presumed dead, and the real Seymour Skinner returns to reclaim it.

Written by Ken Keeler, it drew immediate objections from viewers and from Matt Groening, who criticised it publicly; Keeler has defended it. The episode ends with the town legally restoring the impostor and forbidding further mention of the matter.

ep_trash_of_the_titans.name: Trash of the Titans
ep_trash_of_the_titans.desc:
Broadcast in April 1998. Homer runs for Sanitation Commissioner on an impossible promise, wins, bankrupts the department within a month and leaves the town so buried in refuse that Springfield has to be physically moved.

U2 appear as themselves. The episode won a Primetime Emmy.

ep_behind_the_laughter.name: Behind the Laughter
ep_behind_the_laughter.desc:
Broadcast in May 2000 as the eleventh season finale. A parody of the music documentary format presents the Simpsons as a real family who have been performing a hit television series, complete with addiction, contract disputes and a comeback.

It won a Primetime Emmy, and turned the show's own production history, including its cast's pay negotiations, into the subject of the joke.

tracey_ullman_show.name: The Tracey Ullman Show
tracey_ullman_show.desc:
The Fox sketch series on which the Simpsons first appeared, as short animated interstitials beginning on 19 April 1987.

The shorts were crude, roughly a minute long, and used the same five family members, with Castellaneta and Kavner drawn from the show's own repertory cast. Around fifty were made before the family were given their own half-hour series in 1989.

gracie_films.name: Gracie Films
gracie_films.desc:
James L. Brooks's production company, which has produced The Simpsons throughout its run. Its logo, followed by a short musical sting, closes every episode.

The company's standing in the industry is generally credited with winning the show unusual independence from network interference in its early years.

fox_broadcasting.name: Fox Broadcasting Company
fox_broadcasting.desc:
The network that commissioned and broadcasts the series. Fox was a young fourth network in 1989 with little to lose, which is part of why an animated prime-time comedy for adults was commissioned at all.

The show became the network's defining property and helped establish it as a serious competitor, and Fox later built a Sunday animation block around it.

klasky_csupo.name: Klasky Csupo
klasky_csupo.desc:
The animation studio that produced the Tracey Ullman shorts and the series' first three seasons, giving the early episodes their rougher, more elastic character designs.

The studio's production was replaced from the fourth season, and Klasky Csupo went on to make Rugrats and other series for Nickelodeon.

film_roman.name: Film Roman
film_roman.desc:
The animation studio that took over production of the series from its fourth season, overseeing the cleaner, more consistent look the show has kept since.

Overseas animation work has been carried out by partner studios in Asia throughout, with Film Roman handling the domestic stages of the pipeline.

danny_elfman.name: Danny Elfman
danny_elfman.desc:
Composer of the show's theme, written in 1989 at James L. Brooks's request for something in the mode of 1960s cartoon scoring.

Elfman has said the piece came to him unusually quickly, and it has remained essentially unchanged for the show's entire run, making it one of the most recognisable television themes ever written. He is better known for his film scores, particularly for Tim Burton.

alf_clausen.name: Alf Clausen
alf_clausen.desc:
The series' composer from 1990 until 2017, responsible for its orchestral underscore and for the large majority of its songs, recorded with a full studio orchestra at a time when that had become rare in television.

The producers ended his tenure in 2017, seeking a different musical direction; Clausen subsequently filed an age discrimination suit, which was later settled.

simpsons_movie.name: The Simpsons Movie
simpsons_movie.desc:
The feature film, released in July 2007 after years of development, directed by David Silverman and credited to eleven writers drawn from across the show's history.

Homer's pollution of Springfield's lake leads the government to seal the town under a dome. The film was a substantial commercial success, and its promotional campaign converted a number of American convenience stores into Kwik-E-Marts.

disney_acquisition.name: Disney Acquisition
disney_acquisition.desc:
Disney completed its purchase of 21st Century Fox in March 2019, bringing The Simpsons under Disney ownership while the show continued to air on the Fox network.

The full library was made available on Disney+ at its launch later that year, initially cropped to widescreen in a way that damaged jokes framed for the original format; the service restored the original aspect ratio for the early seasons after complaints.

contract_disputes.name: Cast Contract Disputes
contract_disputes.desc:
The principal voice cast have negotiated collectively several times, most visibly in 1998, 2004, 2008 and 2011, with production halted or delayed on more than one occasion.

In 2011 the studio said the show could not continue without reduced costs, and the cast accepted a pay cut. Harry Shearer briefly announced his departure in 2015 before returning. Behind the Laughter had already turned the negotiations into material years earlier.

opening_sequence.name: The Opening Sequence
opening_sequence.desc:
The title sequence that has opened almost every episode, following each family member across Springfield to converge on the sofa. Its two variable gags, the chalkboard line and the couch, change weekly.

The sequence was reworked when the show moved to high definition in 2009, and guest artists have occasionally been handed the couch gag, including Banksy in 2010 and Guillermo del Toro in 2013.

couch_gag.name: The Couch Gag
couch_gag.desc:
The variable joke that closes the title sequence, in which the family arrive at the sofa and something goes wrong. It began as a small variation and grew into a showcase, sometimes running long enough to alter an episode's timing.

The production has used it to absorb spare running time, to parody other works, and to hand the show over to outside artists for ninety seconds.

chalkboard_gag.name: The Chalkboard Gag
chalkboard_gag.desc:
The line Bart writes repeatedly in detention at the start of most episodes, changing each week. It is one of the show's oldest running jokes and occasionally its most direct channel for commentary.

The production has used it to respond to real events, including the apology to New Orleans after complaints about a song in A Streetcar Named Marge.

doh.name: D'oh!
doh.desc:
Homer's exclamation, which appeared in scripts as a direction for an annoyed grunt rather than as written dialogue. Dan Castellaneta has said he shortened a drawn-out cry used by the comic actor James Finlayson in Laurel and Hardy films.

It was added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2001, defined as an expression of frustration at one's own stupidity, and is the show's most widely adopted contribution to English.

bartmania.name: Bartmania
bartmania.desc:
The merchandising boom of 1990, when Bart's face and catchphrases appeared on an enormous quantity of licensed goods and the character became a genuine cultural phenomenon.

Some American schools banned T-shirts bearing his underachiever slogan, which became a news story in itself and, in the way of such things, sold more shirts. The show's centre of gravity later shifted from Bart to Homer.

do_the_bartman.name: Do the Bartman
do_the_bartman.desc:
A 1990 single credited to Bart Simpson, taken from the album The Simpsons Sing the Blues, whose video was directed by Brad Bird.

It reached number one in the United Kingdom in early 1991. Matt Groening has since said that Michael Jackson co-wrote the song without taking a credit.

treehouse_of_horror.name: Treehouse of Horror
treehouse_of_horror.desc:
The annual Halloween anthology, running since 1990, in which three segments outside the show's continuity parody horror films, science fiction and literature, and in which characters can be killed without consequence.

The format frees the writers from the series' rules entirely, and its recurring conventions include tombstone jokes, alias credits for the crew and an appearance by Kang and Kodos.

steamed_hams.name: Steamed Hams
steamed_hams.desc:
The segment from 22 Short Films About Springfield in which Skinner, having burnt his roast, buys fast food and insists to Superintendent Chalmers that it is his own cooking.

From the mid-2010s it became one of the internet's most heavily remixed pieces of video, recut into thousands of variations, and its popularity long outlived the meme formats around it.

simpsons_predictions.name: The Predictions Phenomenon
simpsons_predictions.desc:
A recurring media story in which moments from old episodes are held up as having predicted later events, most often cited in relation to a 2000 episode showing Lisa succeeding a President Trump, and to a 1998 gag placing a Disney label on the Fox studio.

The explanation usually offered by writers is volume and satire rather than foresight: a show with hundreds of episodes making jokes about plausible futures will occasionally land on one.

bush_waltons.name: The Bush Family Feud
bush_waltons.desc:
In a January 1992 speech, President George H. W. Bush said American families should be more like the Waltons and less like the Simpsons. The show answered within days, adding a line to a rebroadcast in which Bart notes that his family is also praying for an end to the recession.

Barbara Bush had earlier called the show dumb in a magazine interview; the writing staff replied in Marge's voice, and she wrote back apologising.

problem_with_apu.name: The Problem with Apu
problem_with_apu.desc:
A 2017 documentary by the comedian Hari Kondabolu examining the Apu character as a stereotype and its effect on South Asian Americans, drawing on interviews with actors and writers.

The show's on-screen response in 2018 was widely criticised as dismissive. Hank Azaria said in 2020 that he would step away from the role, and the production stopped casting white actors as non-white characters.

emmy_awards.name: Emmy Recognition
emmy_awards.desc:
The series has won more than thirty Primetime Emmy Awards, the bulk of them for Outstanding Animated Program, alongside voice-acting wins for several of its principal cast.

Because of its length it competed in the half-hour animated category for most of its run, and its dominance there was frequently noted when other shows began winning instead.

longest_running_record.name: Longevity Records
longest_running_record.desc:
The Simpsons passed Gunsmoke's twenty seasons in 2009 and its episode total in 2018, making it the longest-running American scripted prime-time series by both measures.

It is also the longest-running American animated series and sitcom. The records are routinely cited in coverage of the show, and the production has marked several of the milestone episodes on screen.

springfield_naming.name: Naming Springfield
springfield_naming.desc:
The town's name is shared with communities in a large number of American states, which is precisely why it was chosen; the show has never named the state and has built running jokes on refusing to.

Matt Groening said in a 2012 interview that he took the name from Springfield, Oregon, near where he grew up, having assumed as a child that the Springfield of Father Knows Best was a real and famous place.

simpsons_did_it.name: Simpsons Did It
simpsons_did_it.desc:
A phrase drawn from a 2002 South Park episode in which a character trying to devise an original scheme finds that The Simpsons has already used every idea.

It captures the position a very long-running comedy eventually occupies, and has been used since by writers on other shows to describe the difficulty of finding a premise the series has not covered.

michael_jackson.name: Michael Jackson
michael_jackson.desc:
Appeared in the 1991 episode Stark Raving Dad, voicing a man in a mental institution who believes he is Michael Jackson. He was credited under the pseudonym John Jay Smith, and a soundalike performed the character's singing.

The producers withdrew the episode from circulation in 2019 following the documentary Leaving Neverland.

dustin_hoffman.name: Dustin Hoffman
dustin_hoffman.desc:
Voiced Mr. Bergstrom, the substitute teacher in Lisa's Substitute, under the pseudonym Sam Etic.

Several early guests took pseudonyms rather than lend their names to a cartoon, a caution the show's later prestige made unnecessary.

paul_mccartney.name: Paul McCartney
paul_mccartney.desc:
Appeared with Linda McCartney in Lisa the Vegetarian, advising Lisa on the roof of the Kwik-E-Mart.

He agreed to appear on condition that Lisa's vegetarianism be permanent rather than reversed at the end of the episode, and the producers have kept to it.

george_harrison.name: George Harrison
george_harrison.desc:
Appeared as himself in Homer's Barbershop Quartet, the episode whose plot maps the Be Sharps onto the Beatles.

With Ringo Starr's earlier appearance and Paul McCartney's later one, three of the four Beatles guest-starred on the show.

ringo_starr.name: Ringo Starr
ringo_starr.desc:
Appeared as himself in the 1991 episode Brush with Greatness, replying at last to a portrait Marge painted of him and sent as a teenager.

The joke rests on his working steadily through decades of accumulated fan mail, and the episode uses it to restore Marge's confidence in her painting.

elizabeth_taylor.name: Elizabeth Taylor
elizabeth_taylor.desc:
Voiced Maggie's first word in the 1992 episode Lisa's First Word, a single syllable spoken after Homer has left the room.

She also appeared as herself in a later episode. The show has kept Maggie effectively silent since, treating her rare words as events.

johnny_cash.name: Johnny Cash
johnny_cash.desc:
Voiced the space coyote that guides Homer through his hallucination in El Viaje Misterioso de Nuestro Jomer.

The casting gives the sequence its gravity: the advice is absurd, and it is delivered in a voice the audience is inclined to believe.

buzz_aldrin.name: Buzz Aldrin
buzz_aldrin.desc:
Appeared as himself in Deep Space Homer, supervising the mission that sends Homer into orbit.

His presence lets the episode make jokes at NASA's expense from inside the institution rather than at a distance.

leonard_nimoy.name: Leonard Nimoy
leonard_nimoy.desc:
Appeared as himself in Marge vs. the Monorail, arriving to open the monorail with no clear reason to be there and vanishing at the end, and returned in the 1997 episode The Springfield Files.

Both appearances trade on his willingness to treat his own iconography as a joke.

james_earl_jones.name: James Earl Jones
james_earl_jones.desc:
Narrated the adaptation of Edgar Allan Poe's The Raven in the first Treehouse of Horror, and returned in later Halloween episodes.

Using a voice of that authority to read Poe straight, over animation of Homer being harassed by a bird with Bart's face, set the anthology's tone of playing the source material seriously.

glenn_close.name: Glenn Close
glenn_close.desc:
Voiced Mona Simpson, Homer's mother, from her introduction in Mother Simpson in 1995 through the character's later appearances.

The casting anchored one of the show's most serious storylines, and she returned for it across more than a decade.

albert_brooks.name: Albert Brooks
albert_brooks.desc:
One of the show's most frequently used guests, often credited as A. Brooks, playing Cowboy Bob, the French tutor Jacques, the self-help guru Brad Goodman and, best known, Hank Scorpio.
