He is widely reported to have improvised heavily in the recording booth, with the writers cutting the results down afterwards.

jon_lovitz.name: Jon Lovitz
jon_lovitz.desc:
A recurring guest across the early seasons, voicing Artie Ziff, the theatre director Llewellyn Sinclair and the con man Aristotle Amadopolis, among others.

His characters share a self-regard the show enjoys puncturing, and Artie Ziff in particular kept returning long after his first appearance.

danny_devito.name: Danny DeVito
danny_devito.desc:
Voiced Herb Powell, Homer's long-lost half-brother, in Oh Brother, Where Art Thou? and its sequel episode.

The first is among the show's earliest attempts at a genuinely sad ending, with Herb ruined by the car he let Homer design.

meryl_streep.name: Meryl Streep
meryl_streep.desc:
Voiced Jessica Lovejoy, the minister's daughter, in the 1994 episode Bart's Girlfriend.

The character is worse behaved than Bart and considerably better at avoiding blame, and the episode ends with him unable to convince anyone of what she has done.

stephen_hawking.name: Stephen Hawking
stephen_hawking.desc:
Appeared as himself in the 1999 episode They Saved Lisa's Brain, arriving to deflate Springfield's chapter of Mensa after it takes over the town, and returned in later episodes.

He was reportedly a viewer of the show, and his appearances are among its most frequently cited guest spots.

tony_bennett.name: Tony Bennett
tony_bennett.desc:
Appeared as himself in the 1990 episode Dancin' Homer, among the earliest celebrities to play themselves on the show.

The brief appearance set the pattern for hundreds that followed, in which the guest is a real person walking through Springfield rather than a voice cast in a role.

john_waters.name: John Waters
john_waters.desc:
Voiced John, the collector of kitsch and camp memorabilia at the centre of Homer's Phobia.

Casting a director known for his own work in camp gave the episode's argument about tolerance a pointed source, and the performance is generally credited with much of why the episode landed as it did.

aerosmith.name: Aerosmith
aerosmith.desc:
Appeared as themselves in Flaming Moe's, playing at the bar after Moe's cocktail makes it fashionable.

They were among the first musical acts to guest on the show, and the appearance began a long line of bands playing versions of themselves in Springfield.

u2.name: U2
u2.desc:
Appeared as themselves in Trash of the Titans, playing a Springfield concert that Homer hijacks to campaign for Sanitation Commissioner.

The sequence parodies the band's own stadium staging, and the episode went on to win a Primetime Emmy.

links.details:
The show's most volatile relationship, and the one it has spent the longest revising. Early seasons played Homer's strangling of Bart as a straight sitcom gag; later ones increasingly framed the pair as alike, with Homer recognising his own worst instincts in his son.

Episodes from Bart the Genius onwards repeatedly end with Bart confessing to a deception and Homer forgiving him, which became one of the series' fixed emotional shapes.

Homer cannot follow anything Lisa cares about, and the show's most reliable source of sincerity is his trying anyway. Lisa's Substitute turns on his failure to be the intellectual company she wants, and on his being the only one there when she needs someone.

The relationship supplies the series with its recurring proof that affection and comprehension are separate things.

And Maggie Makes Three explains that Homer gave up the job he loved and returned to the power plant because Marge was pregnant with her, and ends on the photographs of Maggie he has taped over Burns's demoralising plaque.

Maggie also shoots him nothing, but shoots Mr. Burns, in the resolution the show built an entire summer of publicity around.

Marge is the parent who still believes Bart can be reached, and episodes such as Marge Be Not Proud turn on her withdrawing that belief and on how badly he takes it.

The show frequently uses her disappointment where it would use Homer's anger, because it lands harder.

Marge understands Lisa's intelligence without sharing her convictions, and the friction usually comes from Marge wanting her daughter to be happy rather than right.

Lisa the Vegetarian sets the pattern: Marge's instinct is to smooth the dispute over rather than take a side in it.

Maggie is almost always in Marge's arms or underfoot, and the show has used the pair for its quietest material, including the sequence in Lisa's First Word where Maggie speaks only once Homer has left the room.

The marriage is the show's load-bearing structure: Homer is repeatedly established as an unreasonable proposition and Marge as the person who keeps choosing him anyway.

The Way We Was gives its origin, in a high-school detention and a prom Marge left with the wrong boy. Later episodes have tested it with separations, temptations and one another's ambitions, always returning it intact, and the show has been candid that the reset is a convention rather than a claim about marriage.

Abe is written as the reason Homer is the way he is, and the show has been unusually direct about it: Grampa's neglect is treated as a fact rather than a joke in the episodes that examine it.

Homer parks him in the Springfield Retirement Castle and visits rarely, which the series presents as both cruel and entirely in character.

Mother Simpson reveals that Homer's mother went into hiding after a raid on one of Mr. Burns's laboratories, leaving him to grow up believing she was dead.

Their reunion is broken up by the authorities within the same episode, and the closing shot of Homer alone on his car watching the sky is among the show's most restrained endings.

The marriage ended when Mona went underground in the 1960s. Abe told Homer she was dead, a lie the show treats as the defining act of his parenting and one it does not entirely forgive him for.

They met at a rock concert and married while Abe was already the more conventional of the two; the show places the split at the point where her politics made staying impossible.

When they finally meet again in Mother Simpson, Abe is the one who calls the authorities, which the episode presents as the last thing he can still do to keep her.

Half-brothers, sharing Abe as a father. Herb, given up for adoption, became a Detroit car manufacturer, then sought Homer out and handed him a design brief on the theory that an ordinary man knows what ordinary men want.

The resulting car bankrupts him, and he leaves swearing never to speak to Homer again. A later episode restores his fortune through an invention Homer's money funds, one of the few reversals the show allowed to stand.

Antagonistic by default and unexpectedly loyal under pressure, the pair are written as opposites who understand each other better than either parent understands them.

Lisa's academic success and Bart's failure at the same school is a standing source of friction, and episodes that pair them against an outside threat, as in Lemon of Troy, use the truce for its contrast.

Bart is the sibling Maggie most often imitates, and the show has used the pairing for silent visual gags in which she copies him exactly and gets away with it.

The two share the show's only sibling relationship built entirely on physical comedy, since neither can hold a conversation with the other for different reasons.

Maggie's most decisive act in the series, shooting Mr. Burns, is a compressed version of a Bart plot: an impulsive act with enormous consequences and no punishment.

Lisa treats Maggie as a project, teaching her, testing her and reading meaning into her silences, which the show occasionally rewards by having Maggie prove more capable than anyone realised.

Lisa is the one who notices Maggie, which is a running structural joke in a family where nobody notices anyone. She narrates the baby's inner life on no evidence and is regularly proved right.

The pairing gives the show a way to voice Lisa's loneliness without her having to state it: she talks to the only person in the house who cannot answer.

Patty's contempt for Homer is total and permanent, which puts Marge in the position of defending her marriage to her own family in almost every episode featuring her sisters.

Patty's disapproval extends to the marriage itself rather than to Homer's individual failures, so no amount of good behaviour changes it, and Marge is left arbitrating permanently.

The show has occasionally softened the pattern by having Patty need Marge, most notably when she came out and Marge's difficulty accepting it briefly reversed the usual direction of judgement.

Selma shares Patty's disdain for Homer but wants a marriage of her own, and Marge is repeatedly enlisted in her sister's pursuit of one, with results that include weddings to Sideshow Bob and to Troy McClure.

Twins, near-inseparable, and written as a single unit of smoke and disapproval. The show distinguishes them mainly by Selma's search for a husband and, later, by establishing Patty as a lesbian.

They live together, work together at the Department of Motor Vehicles and holiday together, and the show has repeatedly tested the bond by giving one of them a husband, a child or a secret and watching the arrangement absorb it.

Selma's serial marriages and Patty's long concealment are the two things the twins do not share, and both are used to prise the unit apart for an episode before it closes again.

Jacqueline's disapproval of Homer predates the marriage, and the show has used her sparingly as the source of the Bouvier sisters' shared severity.

The Way We Was shows her steering Marge away from Homer at the point where the decision was still open, which the series treats as the origin of a lifelong grievance on both sides.

Her own late-life marriage to Mr. Burns, called off at the altar, is the one storyline that puts her in Marge's position rather than above it.

Jacqueline raised all three Bouvier sisters, and the show traces the twins' smoke, severity and disappointment directly back to her household.

The show gives the household almost no father, which leaves Jacqueline as the sole source of everything the twins became, cigarettes included.

Patty is the daughter who most resembles her in manner and least in expectation, having abandoned early the pursuit of a husband that her mother treated as the point of a life.

Selma's determination to marry is presented as an inheritance from a mother who valued the institution more than any of the men in it.

Selma's repeated marriages, to Sideshow Bob, Troy McClure, Lionel Hutz and others, are played as a daughter still trying to satisfy a standard nobody has restated in decades.

Her eventual decision to adopt Ling instead resolves the inheritance rather than fulfils it, and the show treats it as the more successful outcome.

Selma adopts Ling from China in Goo Goo Gai Pan, posing as married to satisfy the adoption requirements and taking Homer along as the pretend husband.

It resolves fifteen seasons of Selma wanting a family, and the show has kept Ling rather than reversing it.

Lady Bouvier's Lover pairs the two grandparents, until Mr. Burns takes an interest in Jacqueline and outbids Abe with money and confidence. Abe wins her back at the altar, and the relationship then quietly disappears from the show.

The dog was Bart's first argument for keeping him, in the episode that introduced them both, and subsequent episodes have used the pair for the show's few unqualified affections, including one in which Bart has to win him back after he is trained as a police dog.

Lisa is the cat's nominal owner and the character who mourns her when she is killed off, before immediately acquiring an identical replacement and reusing the name to avoid changing the food bowl.

The gag is one of the show's most efficient jokes about its own resistance to change: grief is permitted for one scene, and then the status quo is restored by simply renaming the replacement.

A later episode extends it into a full family history of cats, all of which died in ways attributable to the household, and Lisa is the only member of it who keeps count.

Moe is Homer's bartender first and confidant second, and the show is careful that the friendship runs through the transaction rather than around it. Moe waters the drinks, adds to the tab and listens.

Flaming Moe's tests it directly: Moe steals Homer's recipe, becomes briefly famous on it, and the friendship survives because neither man has anywhere else to go.

Established as friends since school, and the show has said Barney was a promising student until Homer gave him his first beer, which the series treats as Homer's most consequential act.

Mr. Plow turns the friendship into open commercial war when Barney sets up a rival snowplough business, and Barney's later sobriety is one of the few permanent changes the show has allowed a supporting character.

Colleagues at Sector 7-G and drinking companions at Moe's, in a friendship the show defines almost entirely by proximity: they are in the same room every day and neither has examined it.

Lenny is the friend Homer would not describe as a friend, which is the point: the show is precise about the difference between the people you like and the people you happen to be standing next to for twenty years.

The series has occasionally punctured this, with Homer discovering something substantial about Lenny's life and forgetting it before the next episode.

Carl completes the trio at the plant and the bar, supplying the dry remark to Lenny's earnestness. The show has run a long joke about Homer knowing almost nothing about either of them despite decades of company.

The show treats the two as functionally inseparable, to the point of making the closeness itself a recurring joke, and rarely gives either a scene without the other.

The joke is that the show refuses to define the relationship while making it the most stable one at the plant, and the writing has repeatedly leaned into the ambiguity without settling it.

When an episode does separate them, the plot is almost always about how badly one of them functions alone.

Ned exists to be everything Homer is not, and Homer's resentment of him is written as pure envy dressed up as principle. He borrows Ned's possessions permanently and despises him for lending them.

The show has repeatedly tested the pattern, notably by putting Homer in charge of Ned's welfare after Maude's death, and each time returns the relationship to Homer taking and Ned forgiving.

A conventional churchgoing marriage the show used mainly as a contrast to the Simpsons', until Maude was killed off in 2000 and Ned's widowerhood became a durable part of his character.

The marriage was written as unexamined contentment, which gave the show a stable target: two people whose worst secret is a mildly unfashionable board game collection.

Her death converted Ned from a foil into a character with a wound, and the seasons since have used his search for a second wife as one of the few genuinely open questions among the regulars.

Ned raises his sons on Bible games, prohibitions and a diet free of anything enjoyable, and the show occasionally suggests the results are less serene than he believes.

Ned's own upbringing by permissive beatnik parents, and the spanking-based therapy that followed, is offered as the explanation for how tightly he now runs a household.

The boys are used as the control group for the Simpson children: identical circumstances, opposite parenting, and results that are strange in a different direction.

The show paired Ned and Mrs. Krabappel in its twenty-third season and married them, giving two long-serving supporting characters a genuine change of circumstance.

The marriage ended with Marcia Wallace's death in 2013, after which the producers retired Edna rather than recast her, and Ned's second widowerhood was acknowledged on screen.

Ned's constant telephone calls about minor moral crises are given as the reason Lovejoy stopped caring about his congregation, a piece of backstory the show delivers as a joke and then treats as canon.

In Marge We Trust turns on Lovejoy rediscovering the point of the job.

Barney is Moe's most reliable customer and most permanent fixture, drinking on credit that will never be settled. Barney's decision to stop drinking briefly cost Moe his best trade and the show played the loss as genuine.

Moe has run the bar for the show's entire history, and its condition tracks his: filthy, unprofitable, occasionally remodelled into something fashionable and always restored by the following episode.

Moe's schemes to save the bar have included a family restaurant, a gay bar, a smoking-permitted speakeasy and an English pub, each of which is abandoned by the following episode.

The tavern is also the site of the show's longest-running gag, Bart's prank calls, which Moe answers every time and never anticipates.

Bart's prank calls to the tavern, asking for customers whose names form a joke when Moe shouts them across the bar, are the show's oldest running gag and the closest thing it has to a fixed ritual.

Moe's threats down the phone escalated over the years without ever coming to anything, and later episodes have had him trace the calls, catch Bart, and be defeated anyway.

Apu's shift behind the counter is effectively permanent, a joke the show has made about convenience-store hours since his introduction, and the store's inflated prices and rotating hot dogs are established as his doing rather than a corporate policy.

The Two Mrs. Nahasapeemapetilons brings an arranged marriage agreed in childhood to Springfield, and Apu, having spent the episode trying to escape it, goes through with the wedding and finds it suits him.

A later episode gives them octuplets after fertility treatment, and a still later one separates them over Apu's infidelity before reconciling them.

Homer is the Kwik-E-Mart's most consistent customer and the person Apu is most often obliged to forgive. The friendship carries the plot of Homer and Apu, in which Homer exposes the store's food safety and Apu, sacked, moves in with the Simpsons to make amends.

Smithers's job is total: he manages Burns's business, home, medication and social calendar, and is the only person who can operate the plant's paperwork.

The show played his unrequited love for his employer as innuendo for over twenty years before making it explicit, and Burns's obliviousness to it is presented as of a piece with his obliviousness to everyone.

Smithers's duties include releasing the hounds, operating the trapdoor and reminding Burns which decade it is, and the show has established that the plant would not function for a day without him.

His brief periods away from the job, including one dismissal and one sabbatical, are used to show Burns as genuinely helpless rather than merely eccentric.

Burns cannot retain Homer's name from one episode to the next, asking Smithers who he is after decades of employment, and the joke has outlived almost every other running gag in the show.

The relationship carries the plot of Last Exit to Springfield, in which Homer's accidental union leadership defeats him, and And Maggie Makes Three, in which Burns hangs a plaque over Homer's desk specifically to demoralise him.

Lenny has worked at the plant for the show's entire run without Burns ever learning anything about him, which is the standing condition of employment at Sector 7-G.

Burns's inability to name any employee is a structural joke rather than a character trait, and Lenny is its most frequent demonstration.

The show has twice shown Burns learning something about a worker's life and using it as leverage rather than recognition.

Carl holds a master's degree in nuclear physics and the same grade as Homer, a detail the show drops occasionally to underline how little qualification affects anything at the plant.

Carl is one of the few characters at the plant whose competence is stated on screen and never once acts on it, which the show treats as a comment on the job rather than on him.

He and Lenny are the only workers Burns has occasionally been made to acknowledge, usually by mistake.

Burns hires Grimes after seeing him on television, promotes him on a whim, then demotes him just as arbitrarily to a position alongside Homer, which sets the events of Homer's Enemy in motion.

Grimes's promotion is the plant's normal chaos, but the demotion is the show's decisive move: the one character who earned his position is placed beside the one who did not.

Burns forgets Grimes entirely by the end of the episode, which is the closest the show comes to stating who is responsible for what happens.

Burns's ownership of the plant is the source of his power over the town: it employs a large share of Springfield and poisons the rest of it, and every attempt at regulation in the show founders on his lawyers.

Homer is safety inspector at Sector 7-G, a post he holds without qualification and mostly asleep. The show has removed him from it many times, for astronaut training, a snowplough business, the Globex Corporation and sanitation politics, and always returns him to the same desk.

The three-eyed fish is pulled from the water beside the plant in Two Cars in Every Garage and Three Eyes on Every Fish, and becomes the evidence in a state inspection that Burns evades by running for governor.

Grimes is the only character who reacts to Homer as an outsider would: with disbelief that a man this incompetent has a house, a family, two cars and a job with the word safety in the title.

Homer, who never grasps that he is disliked, tries to befriend him throughout, which makes it worse. Grimes dies attempting to prove a point by imitating him.

Homer's response to open hostility is to invite Grimes to dinner, which the episode presents as the cruellest thing he could have done.

The funeral, at which Homer sleeps through the eulogy and the mourners laugh, is the bleakest joke the show has made about its own central character.

Scorpio is the best employer Homer has ever had: he learns his name, values his work, asks after his family and puts him in charge of people.

He is also seizing the East Coast with a doomsday device, which Homer never notices. The episode's joke is that the supervillainy is incidental and the management is sincere.

The fixed antagonism of Springfield Elementary. Skinner's authority depends entirely on containing one pupil, and the show has him lose his job, his dignity and occasionally his mind to Bart across dozens of episodes.

The relationship is written as mutual dependence: episodes that separate them tend to show both men adrift.

Skinner lives with his mother in middle age and is undermined by her at every turn, a relationship the show treats as the explanation for everything else about him.

The Principal and the Pauper puts it under the greatest strain by revealing that they are not related at all, and ends with Agnes choosing the impostor over her real son.

A long, intermittent affair conducted in supply cupboards and staff rooms, which the show advanced and reset for years before eventually marrying Edna to Ned Flanders instead.

The affair is the school's open secret and its most reliable source of humiliation, since both parties are found out by children with no interest in discretion.

The show ended it by marrying Edna to Ned Flanders, a resolution that also quietly acknowledged Skinner would never leave his mother's house.

Chalmers arrives to inspect, is lied to, and leaves in disgust; the pattern is the school's most reliable comic engine.

Their lunch in 22 Short Films About Springfield, in which Skinner passes off fast food as home cooking while his kitchen burns, later became one of the most reworked pieces of footage on the internet.

Skinner's whole life is the school: he lives with his mother, eats in the staff room and defends a budget that cannot cover asbestos removal, and the institution has worn him down as thoroughly as it has his teachers.

Mrs. Krabappel's exhaustion is presented as the school's product rather than her temperament: an underfunded institution has worn away a teacher who once expected something better.

The staff room is written as a place where teachers have stopped pretending, and Mrs. Krabappel's cynicism is the least performative version of it.

Her few attempts to reach individual pupils, particularly Bart and Nelson, are among the show's most restrained scenes, and none of them are allowed to work permanently.

Willie lives in a shack on the school grounds and is conscripted into every task the budget cannot cover, from boiler repairs to substitute teaching, at wages the show implies are barely legal.

The show has repeatedly used him as the school's actual emergency service, sending him after escaped pupils, wolves and, in one case, a fire he is expected to fight alone.

His relationship with Skinner runs on undisguised contempt that neither the pay nor the pretence of hierarchy has ever reduced.

Mrs. Krabappel has taught Bart's fourth-grade class for the show's entire run, a permanence the series jokes about directly.

Her assessments of him are accurate and delivered without hope, and Bart Gets an F turns on the one occasion she tells him he has genuinely learned something.

Milhouse sits in the same fourth-grade class as Bart and absorbs the consequences of his schemes, which Mrs. Krabappel has long since stopped trying to separate.

Milhouse is the pupil whose punishments are usually collateral, since he is beside Bart when the scheme is discovered and slower to leave the room.

The class supplies the show with its fixed social geography, and Milhouse's position in it, adjacent to the troublemaker and beneath the bullies, has not changed in three decades.

Nelson is in Mrs. Krabappel's class, and the show has used her attempts to reach him for its rare glimpses of his home life.

Her interventions with Nelson are among the few times the show lets a teacher succeed even briefly, usually by treating him as a child rather than as a disciplinary problem.

The results never survive past the episode, which the series presents as a statement about the school rather than about him.

Martin is the only pupil who answers her questions, which the show plays as a burden on the teacher rather than a relief.

Martin's enthusiasm is written as an irritant to everyone in the room including the teacher, which lets the show satirise the classroom's reward structure from both ends.

His academic rivalry with Lisa plays out largely in front of Mrs. Krabappel, who is uniformly unimpressed by both.

The twins sit behind Bart and supply the class's running commentary on his failures, usually in unison.

The twins function as the class's chorus, announcing Bart's failures in unison and with evident satisfaction, usually within seconds of them occurring.

They are also the show's most economical device for exposition, since anything the audience needs to know about the school's pecking order can be said by two children at once.

Bart's best friend and the reliable casualty of his plans. Milhouse supplies the loyalty, absorbs the punishment and receives none of the credit, and the show has been explicit that the friendship is unequal.

Bart Sells His Soul begins with Milhouse buying the soul for five dollars and refusing to sell it back, the one occasion he holds the advantage.

Milhouse's hopeless devotion to Lisa runs the length of the series, is periodically acknowledged by her and never returned. The show has used it for some of its bleakest jokes about persistence.

Lisa is aware of it, addresses it directly on several occasions and declines each time without cruelty, which the show treats as the more honest outcome.

A handful of episodes have granted him a brief reciprocation before withdrawing it, and the pattern has become one of the series' longest sustained jokes about hope.

Kirk's divorce and subsequent decline are largely observed through their effect on Milhouse, who shuttles between parents and reports each humiliation to Bart.

Kirk's job at the cracker factory, his eviction to a single-room flat and his failed singing career are all filtered through Milhouse's embarrassment rather than presented directly.

The show has reconciled the parents more than once and separated them again, using Milhouse each time as the measure of what it costs.

After the divorce Milhouse divides his time between his mother's house and his father's bachelor flat, and reports each new indignity to Bart.

Luann's post-divorce life, including the American Gladiator she dates, is played mostly for Milhouse's reaction to it.

She is one of the few parents on the show written as visibly happier after a marriage ends, which the series does not treat as a failing.

A Milhouse Divided separates them at a dinner party, and Homer, watching, panics about his own marriage and remarries Marge by way of reassurance. Kirk's attempts to recover afterwards are played as sustained humiliation.

Nelson's beatings of Bart established the school's pecking order in the early seasons, and the two later settled into an uneasy alliance in which Bart supplies the schemes and Nelson the threat of violence.

Milhouse is Nelson's most convenient target, small enough to be beaten without effort and reliable enough to be found in the same place every day.

The bullying is presented as routine maintenance rather than malice, and Milhouse's acceptance of it is what makes the joke sit uncomfortably.

When the two are forced into alliance the show plays Nelson as the more competent partner, which does nothing to change the arrangement afterwards.

Martin is Lisa's only academic equal at the school, which makes him her rival in every contest the plot supplies, and the show uses him to show that being right is not the same as being sympathetic.

Their competition covers science fairs, elections, orchestra chairs and grades, and the show usually resolves it by having something outside the classroom matter more.

Martin's fate at the hands of the other children is the show's standing note on what academic success costs at that age, and Lisa's relative safety from it is never explained.

The affection between them is uncomplicated and, by the show's standards, unusually warm: Wiggum is proud of a son who cannot follow a sentence, and the series lets that stand without undercutting it.

Wiggum arrests Snake at the end of most of his appearances and loses him again before the next, an arrangement the show treats as a stable equilibrium rather than a failure.

Snake's escapes are rarely shown, which is the joke: the show does not consider the police force worth the exposition.

On the occasions Wiggum does catch him properly, the arrest is either accidental or the result of Snake stopping to gloat.

Bob spent years as Krusty's mute stooge, pelted with pies and fired from cannons, and his contempt for that treatment is the stated motive for framing his employer for armed robbery in Krusty Gets Busted.

The show has returned to the grievance repeatedly, with Bob's cultural refinement set against the crude television he was forced to serve.

Mel replaced Bob and has served without incident since, which the show notes is the only reason he lacks a criminal record.

Mel is a trained Shakespearean actor reduced to being hit with a plank, and the show occasionally lets his diction remind the audience of the fact.

Unlike Bob, he has never attempted revenge, which the series presents as the difference between resentment expressed and resentment endured.

Bart's testimony sent Bob to prison in his first appearance, and the pursuit that followed has run for over thirty years across roughly a dozen episodes.

Cape Feare is its fullest expression, with Bob paroled, following the family into witness protection, and defeated by his own inability to resist a flourish. The show has repeatedly given him the chance to kill Bart and had him talk himself out of it.

Bob marries Selma in Black Widower, having courted her from prison, and intends to kill her for her money; Bart works it out during the honeymoon broadcast. It is the first of Selma's several disastrous marriages.

Bart is Krusty's most devoted viewer, and the show mines the gap between the performer's on-screen warmth and his private contempt for children.

Bart and Lisa clear him of the Kwik-E-Mart robbery, and later episodes have Bart rescue his career more than once, always without changing his opinion of the audience.

The cartoon runs inside Krusty's programme, which lets the show satirise children's television and the licensing around it in the same scene: Krusty screens the violence, sells the merchandise and takes none of the blame.

Poochie is added to the cartoon by executives demanding something new for a stale format, and killed off in the same episode at the audience's insistence.

The episode is the show's most direct answer to demands that it freshen itself, and Poochie's name is now used generally for a character added to save a franchise.

Comic Book Guy's denunciation of the Poochie episode as the worst thing he has ever seen, and Bart's reply that he is getting it for free, is the show arguing with its own audience in public and giving both sides the best line available.

Bart and Milhouse are the Android's Dungeon's main custom, and Comic Book Guy alternates between contempt for their taste and dependence on their pocket money.

The Android's Dungeon is where Bart's schemes are financed and where his collectibles are valued at a fraction of what he paid.

Comic Book Guy's contempt is aimed at the customers he depends on, which the show uses as its most direct joke about the economics of fandom.

Radioactive Man is the comic Bart and Milhouse collect, and the 1995 episode about its film adaptation casts Milhouse as the sidekick Fallout Boy, ruining the production and the friendship in the same week.

Murphy is the first adult to take Lisa's playing seriously, meeting her on a bridge in the first season when she is miserable and playing with her instead of consoling her.

His death in Round Springfield gives the show its most sustained treatment of grief, ending with Lisa hearing him one last time in the clouds.

Lisa's brief romance with the school bully, in which she sets out to reform him and mostly succeeds until his friends reappear. The show uses it to fill in Nelson's home life, and to make his eventual reversion sadder than it is funny.

Marge's prom date in The Way We Was, who behaves badly enough in a parked car that she walks home, then returns across later seasons as a wealthier man still convinced she chose wrong.

Artie's later appearances turn the grievance into a running study of a man who has confused wealth with vindication, offering Marge his fortune, his company and, eventually, a life-sized replica of her.

The show consistently gives him the better circumstances and Homer the marriage, which is the entire point of the character.

Quimby's administration is the show's standing joke about local government: policy is set by whoever shouted last at a town meeting, and the treasury is emptied by whatever scheme the town has just been sold, from a monorail to a legalised casino.

The two towns split, in the founding myth the show supplies in Lemon of Troy, over an irreconcilable disagreement between Jebediah Springfield and Shelbyville Manhattan about what the new settlement would permit.

The rivalry supplies episodes with a ready-made enemy who is identical to Springfield in every respect, which is the joke.

The plant dominates the town physically and economically, and most of Springfield's environmental disasters, mutations and inspection farces originate there.

Its safety record is the town's running joke and its economic dependence the reason nothing is ever done about it, a relationship the show established in the first season and has never resolved.

The plant is also the source of Blinky, the three-eyed fish that gave the series its first sustained environmental storyline.

The school is the town's most visibly underfunded institution, and much of the show's satire of American public education runs through its corridors.

Its budget crises drive entire episodes, from selling advertising space on pupils to closing the music programme, and the staff are written as people managing decline rather than teaching.

The school also supplies the show's fixed child cast, which is why almost every plot involving Bart or Lisa passes through it at some point.

The Kwik-E-Mart is where Springfield buys everything at the last minute and at the worst price, and where the town's petty crime is most often committed.

It is open at every hour the plot requires, prices are set by whatever Apu thinks he can get, and the hot-dog rollers have been running since the first season.

The store is also the show's most durable setting for satire of convenience retail, from expired stock to the surveillance archive Apu keeps of his customers.

Moe's is Springfield's least appealing bar and its most reliable social institution, the room the show sends Homer to whenever a plot needs him out of the house.

The bar is where the show puts its adult male cast when it needs them in one room, which makes it the town's real forum: elections, feuds and business schemes all begin there.

Its patrons are the show's fixed chorus, and their unanimity about anything is usually the signal that it is a bad idea.

The church gathers almost the entire cast in one room every Sunday, which makes it the show's most convenient setting for town-wide satire of American religious life.

Attendance is treated as automatic rather than devout, and the show gets much of its comedy from the gap between the congregation's presence and its attention.

The building has burned down, been rebuilt with corporate sponsorship and briefly been run by Ned Flanders, each of which the series used to satirise a different aspect of American religious institutions.

The minister's wife runs the town's gossip and its moral panics, and her appeal that somebody think of the children has passed into general English use as shorthand for substituting sentiment for an argument.

Lovejoy preaches to a congregation he has stopped expecting anything from, and refers pastoral emergencies to the church answering machine.

In Marge We Trust gives the burnout a cause: years of Ned Flanders telephoning about trivial scruples wore down a minister who arrived with genuine enthusiasm.

The same episode returns him to the job by having him rescue Ned from a baboon enclosure, which the show offers without irony as the restoration of a vocation.

Ned is the congregation's most committed member, running the Sunday school, volunteering for everything and telephoning the minister at home about scruples nobody else has noticed.

Ned's faith is written as sincere rather than hypocritical, which is what makes him usable: the show satirises the institution around him without making him its instrument.

His crisis after Maude's death, in which he briefly loses it entirely, is one of the few times the series has treated belief as something that can be taken away.

Duffman is the brewery's mascot, and the show has repeatedly established that the man inside the costume is replaceable while the character is contractually immortal.

The show has established that the role passes between men, that at least one has died in it and that the character is required by contract to continue regardless.

He is also the show's most direct joke about advertising as a job: a person whose entire vocabulary is a slogan and who is not permitted to stop.

Duff is Homer's fixed appetite and the show's vehicle for satire of brewing and advertising, including the brewery tour that reveals Duff, Duff Lite and Duff Dry all flow from the same pipe.

The brewery tour in Duffless is the show's clearest statement of the relationship: Homer is shown the fraud in detail and it changes nothing about his consumption.

Duff also supplies the series with a fixed satirical target for sports sponsorship, mascots and mass-market brewing, all of which Homer accepts uncritically.

The show's two physicians are exact opposites: Hibbert is competent and unmoved, chuckling through terminal diagnoses, while Dr. Nick is warm, cheap and dangerous. Characters choose between them according to what the plot needs to go wrong.

Frink teaches at Springfield Heights Institute of Technology and is the town's only source of advanced technology, which is why every plot requiring a doomsday device, a time machine or a hover car routes through his laboratory first.

Bart is briefly taken into the mob's employ in Bart the Murderer, delivering packages he does not understand, and Fat Tony treats him with the same elaborate courtesy he extends to everyone he is about to implicate.

Wiggum's police force and Fat Tony's organisation coexist comfortably, with arrests made only when a plot requires them, which the show presents as the natural condition of both institutions.

Wiggum has attended Fat Tony's dinners, taken his money and arrested him in the same season without the show treating any of it as inconsistent.

Bart the Murderer puts the arrangement at its most explicit, with a trial that collapses because the judge, the jury and the police are all compromised in different directions.

Moleman is Springfield's most disposable citizen, crushed, buried or launched whenever a scene needs a casualty, and present again in the next crowd shot without explanation.

He has been buried alive, set on fire, driven into a wall and shot into space, and the show has never acknowledged that any of it should have been fatal.

A running gag establishes him as far younger than he appears, with the damage attributed to alcohol, which the series delivers once and never repeats.

The bus driver is the only adult who treats Bart as a peer, which the show presents as evidence about Otto rather than about Bart.

Otto's licence, his living arrangements and his fitness to drive children are all running jokes the school has repeatedly failed to resolve.

The show uses him as Bart's window into a version of adulthood with no responsibilities attached, and is careful to show that it has not worked out well.

Willie's contempt for his employer is undisguised and survives every reconciliation, and Skinner's authority over him lasts only as long as the school's budget can pay him.

Willie's job description expands with every budget cut, which the show plays as a standing negotiation conducted at maximum volume in a boiler room.

Skinner's authority collapses whenever Willie is genuinely needed, and both characters understand this well before the audience is told.

The older bullies outrank Bart and Nelson both, and are usually found outside the Kwik-E-Mart. Running jokes establish Kearney as far older than his classmates, with a car, a divorce and a son of his own.

Gil drifts through Springfield's businesses selling houses, cars and copiers, failing at each in turn, and is the town's standing reminder that its economy has a bottom.

Gil was written as a parody of the desperate salesman of American drama and has since become the show's most reliable measure of a bad situation: if Gil is doing better than you, the plot has gone wrong.

He is one of the few recurring characters the series has never allowed a genuine success.

Abernathy is a fixture of Springfield's streets, communicating by shrieking and throwing cats, until a later episode retrofits her with a name and a history as a burnt-out doctor and lawyer.

The retrofit is characteristic of the show's later method: a background joke given a biography that makes it less comfortable without removing it.

Her few intelligible lines are usually the most lucid thing said in the scene, which is the joke the later writing found in her.

Cletus and his family live on the town's rural fringe and supply its broadest class comedy, introduced with an on-screen caption identifying him as a slack-jawed yokel.

The Spuckler children, numbering somewhere in the dozens and named at speed, are the show's most frequently repeated version of the joke.

Later seasons have occasionally undercut it by giving Cletus a competence the town lacks, particularly in anything agricultural.

Wolfcastle's McBain films and Krusty's programme belong to the same Springfield entertainment industry, and the show pairs the two whenever it wants a celebrity panel, a telethon or a roast.

Wolfcastle's career decline runs on a longer arc than Krusty's, taking in a family film, a sitcom and eventually a run for office, all of which the show treats as the same failure in different costumes.

The McBain films exist within the series as a fixed cultural background, quoted by characters who have clearly seen them many times.

Brockman's Channel 6 broadcasts are how Springfield learns what has happened to it, which means the town's understanding of any crisis is filtered through a man who will say whatever holds an audience and change sides the moment power does.

Castellaneta has said the voice began as an impression of Walter Matthau, which he could not sustain through a full recording session, and settled into a higher, looser register as Homer's writing grew broader.

The performance carries the show's single most recognisable sound, the annoyed grunt written into scripts as a stage direction rather than a word.

Grampa's voice is pitched as an exhausted, wavering version of Homer's, which quietly supports the show's argument that Homer is becoming his father.

Castellaneta plays Grampa's digressions at a speed that suggests the character has stopped expecting to be interrupted, which is how the show gets pathos out of a joke about boring old men.

The two roles are frequently in scene together, and the recording is done by switching between them in the same session.

Krusty's rasp is Homer's voice pushed through decades of cigarettes, a resemblance the show has occasionally acknowledged in the writing.

Krusty on air and Krusty off air are pitched differently, and the drop between them carries most of the character's satire of children's entertainment.

Castellaneta has said the voice began as an impression of a Chicago children's television host rather than of a clown.

Barney is built around a belch, and Castellaneta's performance shifted noticeably when the show made the character sober, giving him a clearer and more melancholy register.

The belch was originally performed rather than sampled, and it became the character's entire introduction for several seasons.

When the show sobered him up in 2000 it gave Castellaneta room for a clearer register, and the performance is what made the change legible before the writing explained it.

Quimby's accent is a broad Kennedy impression, which the writing uses to carry the show's satire of American political dynasties without ever naming one.

The accent does the satire on its own: the show rarely has to specify what the mayor is guilty of, because the voice has already suggested the category.

Quimby's public statements are delivered with the same cadence whether he is opening a library or admitting to embezzlement.

The Scottish accent has been the subject of long-running complaint and equally long-running use, and Castellaneta plays it at a volume that makes the character's rage its own punchline.

Castellaneta reportedly arrived at the accent after the character was written without one specified, and it fixed Willie's entire personality in a single reading.

The show has twice acknowledged the complaint on screen, once by having Willie address the audience directly about it.

Moleman's frail wheeze is pitched as far from Homer as Castellaneta's range goes, and the joke of the character depends on it sounding too old to survive whatever is about to happen to him.

The voice is the only thing establishing the character's supposed age, since the design was originally drawn as a much younger man.

It also carries the show's most reliable structural joke: whatever is about to happen to Moleman, he will explain it politely first.

Gil's whine was written as a replacement for the salesman-adjacent roles lost when Phil Hartman died, and Castellaneta pitches it just short of tears in every scene.

Gil was introduced in 1998, the year Phil Hartman died, and the show has been open about the character filling a gap in its roster of failing salesmen.

Castellaneta plays him as a man narrating his own collapse in real time, which is why the character works better in small doses than in whole episodes.

Mel is played in a booming theatrical register that never drops, on or off air, which is the whole of the character: Krusty's replacement sidekick takes the work far more seriously than his employer does.

Within the episode Homer is cast as Poochie, so Castellaneta is playing a character playing a character, and the layered performance is part of the satire of network casting.

Homer is cast as Poochie inside the episode, so the performance is a man playing a character playing a dog written by a focus group.

The layering is the point of the satire: everyone involved knows the character is worthless and nobody involved can say so.

Kavner's natural rasp defines the character, and the writers built Marge's patience and her occasional breaking point around a voice that already sounds like it has been holding something in.

She has won a Primetime Emmy for the role and, unusually among the cast, rarely performs it in public.

Kavner voices both twins as well as Marge, distinguishing the sisters by pushing the same rasp lower and flatter, so that the Bouvier household sounds like one voice worn three ways.

Kavner's own voice, made rough by a permanent condition of the vocal cords, is the reason all four Bouvier women sound related without any effect being applied.

She records the sisters in conversation with each other and with Marge, sometimes in the same take.

Selma is Marge's rasp pushed lower and more resigned, and Kavner distinguishes the twins largely through how much hope each voice still contains.

Selma is the twin the show gives the storylines to, and Kavner pitches her marginally warmer than Patty to make room for them.

The adoption of Ling is played almost entirely in the voice, since the animation gives Selma no new expressions to work with.

Kavner plays the Bouvier matriarch as a thinner, more brittle version of the same voice she gives all three daughters, so the family sounds like a single disapproval passed down a generation.

The matriarch's voice is thinner and more precise than her daughters', which lets the show suggest a generation of enforced propriety without writing a line about it.

Kavner therefore plays every member of Marge's family, so any Bouvier scene is recorded entirely by one performer.

Cartwright has said she auditioned for Lisa and asked to read for Bart after seeing a character description she found more interesting, and got the part in the room.

She has won a Primetime Emmy for the role and later wrote a memoir about playing a ten-year-old boy for decades.

Nelson's two-syllable jeer is one of the show's most imitated sounds, and Cartwright performs the bully in the same register she uses for his principal victim.

Cartwright voices both the bully and his principal victim's best friend's best friend, which means she frequently plays several sides of a playground scene at once.

Nelson's laugh has been isolated as a stock sound far beyond the show, and the performance keeps it just short of malice.

Ralph's lines are delivered with complete serenity, which is what makes them work: Cartwright never plays the joke, only the child's certainty that what he is saying makes sense.

Ralph began as a background pupil with no fixed characterisation, and the voice is largely what turned him into one of the show's most quoted characters.

The delivery is what makes his line about Lisa breaking his heart work as the only genuinely sad moment in an episode otherwise built on him being funny.

Cartwright voices Todd, the younger Flanders boy, opposite Pamela Hayden's Rod, giving the pair the flat obedience that makes their rare lapses funny.

Cartwright and Pamela Hayden split the Flanders boys between them, playing them as a matched pair whose obedience is total until it is not.

Todd's rare lapses, including a swear word and a brief loss of faith after his mother's death, are the show's most efficient use of a two-line character.

Smith's own speaking voice is close to Lisa's, and she is the only member of the principal cast who regularly voices a single character rather than a stable of them.

She has won a Primetime Emmy for the role, which requires her to carry most of the show's earnest material without letting it turn sentimental.

Azaria has described the voice as built from an actor's gravelly delivery, and it has darkened with the character, who has become the show's most despairing regular.

The character has darkened considerably over the run, and the voice has followed, moving from a bar-owner's bark to something closer to permanent despair.

Azaria plays Moe's rare moments of tenderness in the same register as the threats, which is why they land as unsettling rather than sentimental.

The police chief's voice is a broad, adenoidal drawl that Azaria has said he based on the actor Edward G. Robinson.

Azaria has said the voice is an impression of Edward G. Robinson, which is why a police chief who has never solved anything sounds like a 1930s gangster.

The register also does the character's parenting: the same voice used on Ralph is the show's shortest route to why Ralph is the way he is.

Azaria voiced Apu from the first season until 2020. The portrayal drew sustained criticism as a stereotype, examined in the 2017 documentary The Problem with Apu, and Azaria said publicly that he had come to understand the objections and would step away from the role.

Comic Book Guy's flat, over-enunciated sarcasm gives the show a voice for its own most exacting viewers, and Azaria delivers the superlatives as though reading a verdict.

The character's superlatives, delivered as verdicts, gave the show a way to include its own critics in the joke without answering them.

Azaria based the delivery on a college housemate, and the flat over-enunciation is what makes the catchphrase quotable rather than merely sarcastic.

Azaria has described the performance as derived from Jerry Lewis's Nutty Professor, complete with the trailing nonsense syllables the character produces under any pressure.

The trailing syllables function as a stress response: the more the invention fails, the less of the sentence survives.
